As with all attempts by Drukhari to grow in power, @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-actors.Actor.KZk1yGduhULvMbmP]{Varon}’s attempts are watched with a mixture of approval, disgust, and caution. Any who rise too fast are quickly thrown down, and Varon has begun to suspect that his Archon’s ‘tests’ are little more than an attempt to put him in his place.

Resources

The Dripping Fang Kabal as a whole operates through Webway portals hidden in the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.B7MZBBT3bNew9N96.JournalEntryPage.d0lv2v4FkeIb43jj]{Drimor Subsector}, particularly around @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.B7MZBBT3bNew9N96.JournalEntryPage.nLrpWOo3BjHLB0FG]{Proteus Secundus, Quartus and Quintus}. Through his old ties and lost family secrets, @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-actors.Actor.KZk1yGduhULvMbmP]{Varon }has a handful of other Webway portals he keeps secret, particularly on @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.B7MZBBT3bNew9N96.JournalEntryPage.59y8WFXTbwKRwiRI]{Voll}, near Hive Sanksorak, under the rule of @UUID[Compendium.impmal-starter-set.journals.JournalEntry.Vjfxkwi1rFYPnSIf.JournalEntryPage.Dml6BI69jLrNOQU0#vylathi]{House Vylathi}. Knowing where these portals are located would be invaluable to the Inquisition to shut Varon down. However, if pressured, Varon would likely give up the Kabal’s portals in Drimor before sacrificing his own.

Among the few favours @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-actors.Actor.KZk1yGduhULvMbmP]{Varon }has yet to exhaust is the services of a Haemonculus outside the Dripping Fang’s influence. Klaevus Varaan has worked several times as a healer for Varon and his Kabalites, but Varon retains Klaevus’ services for the pact he made with a @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-actors.Actor.uybcmaEfabyk4D4R]{Mandrake} assassin, whom Varon calls upon for desperate operations. The Mandrake is a nightmarish creature that lives within the shadows and feeds upon the pain and terror of its prey, making it a nigh-perfect assassin.

Varon’s squad has around twenty @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-actors.Actor.b8x4YQfSyzlvU4LX]{Drukhari Kabalite Warriors}, and more seek to join his cause every day.

Methods

@UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-actors.Actor.KZk1yGduhULvMbmP]{Varon} has made several deals with Humans in the Macharian Sector to grow his power base and influence, avoiding the roadblocks within the Kabal that would now withhold power from him. He targets overambitious leaders within the Imperium's planetary governance — heads of noble houses or leaders within the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.3TtxuCzt0nNV1ysj]{Administratum}. He offers mercenary work in trade for information and throngs of pitiless captives he can claim for the Kabal’s pits, more lives than his band of Kabalite warriors could claim through raiding alone.

@UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-actors.Actor.KZk1yGduhULvMbmP]{Varon }often claims to have more power than he realistically has, leaning on his family’s legacy or frequently outright lying to strike deals in his favour. Only some Drukhari, those higher up in the Dripping Fang, routinely see through his bluffs. The Humans he deals with are none the wiser, and many believe Varon commands a sizeable xenos army.

Secrets

@UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-actors.Actor.KZk1yGduhULvMbmP]{Varon }has another master he must, for now, serve: Dracon Sykil Xulfur, leader of the Splinter of the Blood Toxicant, of which his squad serves under in the Kabal’s hierarchy. Varon knows he will have to kill her one day to claim his rightful place, but until then, he must tolerate her orders. Similarly, Sykil knows who Varon is and must humiliate him to ensure his power within the Splinter does not grow enough to overcome her. Sykil often sends Varon on hopeless or deadly missions, preventing him from pursuing his true goal.

@UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-actors.Actor.KZk1yGduhULvMbmP]{Varon }seeks a @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.xxcZ1PUz0t1ycevK.JournalEntryPage.GyAY9bnCmCZ3JjzK#drukhari]{Drukhari} artefact that once belonged to Archon Vypar S’Threil and was thought to be destroyed — a Nightmare Doll. These twisted talismans are exceedingly rare and difficult to construct, created explicitly for one owner, and absorb the injuries they might suffer on the battlefield. Varon believes that recovering the Nightmare Doll will improve his position with the Archon. However, the Haemonculus Klaevus Varaan claims he can reverse the Doll’s effects and wield it as a weapon against the Archon. Varon knows the Archon lost the Doll somewhere in the Macharian Sector and that an Ordo Xenos Inquisitor discovered it. Varon is unsure how he will use the Doll but is trading for any information on the Inquisition to recover it.

pages.name: Xandro Cosmar & Ankhet
pages.text:
Xandro Cosmar & Ankhet

Look out into the void and the stars, my friend. Anything and everything out there can be yours. You just have to want it bad enough.

Threat Overview

  • Xandro Cosmar is a Rogue Trader and Commander of the battlecruiser Mortiferum Ludum, accompanied by his heretek advisor, the Tech-Priest Ankhet.

  • Together, the pair form a cunning alliance: the overwhelming resources and freedom of movement afforded to a Rogue Trader, combined with a rogue Tech-Priest’s genius.

  • Their ambitions are simple: to collect and study xenos artefacts discovered across distant worlds, using the guise of Imperium-approved xenocide as a cover for securing their plunder.

Claiming descent from a long line of wealth stretching to the days before the Horus Heresy, Xandro Cosmar is a man accustomed to getting what he wants and has no qualms about using anything to get it. As a Rogue Trader and Commander of the Overlord-class battlecruiser Mortiferum Ludum, Xandro has seen decades of service to the Imperium as a vanguard, seeking out new planets and exterminating any native intelligent life for the Emperor’s glory. He pursues this path not out of a sense of patriotism, but calculated greed.

He is a dashing example of Rogue Trader propaganda. Despite decades of service, rejuvenat treatments have ensured that Xandro has retained much of his youthful looks. He prefers his long, jet-black hair tied back in a low ponytail and dresses in fashionable and elaborate clothing well suited for society functions or commanding the bridge. He sees himself as a cross between a collector of fine goods and a hunter of dangerous game. Having collected vast wealth and accolades, Xandro has grown bored of what the Imperium can provide within its borders, instead favouring his unparalleled freedom of travel, seeking out new and unknown worlds to plunder for novelties to add to his teeming collections.

Xandro does not just collect xenos artefacts but also maintains a hidden menagerie of xenos creatures in the Mortiferum Ludum for his amusement. A few of these wretched beasts are the last of their kind, so enthusiastically did Xandro hunt them to extinction. All are trophies, a personal tally of his exploits that, in his own mind at least, add to the glory of his name.

Xandro is driven by the desire for others to recognise his own presumed magnificence. He sees himself as a clear successor to the deeds of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.B7MZBBT3bNew9N96.JournalEntryPage.X5EFP7IgIUx6CaBW]{Lord Solar Macharius}. Like the fabled hero, Xandro knows he has the will to bring hundreds of worlds to heel. Unlike the Lord Solar, Xandro has little qualms about using xenos technologies to achieve his objectives and sees himself as an innovator in this aspect, defying both the Lex Imperialis and the Imperial Creed in one heretical swoop. To him, the Macharian Crusade was a blueprint, one he could improve upon, and Xandro has absolute faith that it is only a matter of time before his conquests spark a new wave of zealots ready to follow him into the great unknown.

The Rogue Trader has already begun collecting a cadre of admirers willing to follow him beyond the limits of the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.3mzwixuzgerGUpu1.JournalEntryPage.7wLH7EP0cj0I6T30]{Astronomican}. Chief among his staff is his heretek advisor, Ankhet. In stark contrast to the Rogue Trader’s unsullied flesh, Ankhet is a heavily augmented Tech-Priest, having performed countless surgeries upon himself to the point that his silhouette is barely Human. Ankhet skitters along using a dozen or so appendages underneath his red robes, his visage is a cluster of unblinking eye lenses that twist and focus, surrounded by cables, tubes and vents.

Despite their physical differences, Xandro recognised a kindred sadistic spirit in Ankhet. It did not take long for the two to strike a bargain. In exchange for Ankhet’s extensive knowledge of xenos technology and his heretical willingness to employ it to the Rogue Trade’s benefit, Xandro would take the Tech-Priest to the fringes of the Macharian Sector to continue his research away from the prying eyes of his @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.nYfLVXh10BKR47Kj]{Mechanicus} brethren and the Inquisition.

Use the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-actors.Actor.ipcjevVXtDR4XkNu]{Voidship Captain} stat-block to represent Xandro Cosmar, and the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-actors.Actor.rilaQaBPslIRzGco]{Tech-Priest} stat-block to represent Ankhet.

Resources

The Mortiferum Ludum carries a full complement of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-actors.Actor.pXsZLEawZr8Tf8Ym]{Armsmen}, who are acclimated to dangerous combat engagements in various hostile conditions. Ankhet is typically accompanied by @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-actors.Actor.KTlRprKRb8XzlnAD]{Gun Servitors}, which he custom-builds for each mission.

Xandro is also extremely wealthy and understands the value of using money to overcome most obstacles. Bribery comes to him naturally, as he needs officials to look the other way, and he has amassed countless favours from agents across the Adeptus Terra to make his life easier. Xandro might even be owed a favour with the characters' Patron. Xandro does not hide his wealth and is often adorned with trophies taken from the various xenos creatures — or species — that have died in his conquests. His most prized piece is a matched pair of bracelets bearing what he claims to be authentic @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.xxcZ1PUz0t1ycevK.JournalEntryPage.GyAY9bnCmCZ3JjzK#aeldari]{Aeldari} spirit stones, but he is not beyond parting with such pieces if they can save his neck, especially as there are some things solars cannot buy.

Ankhet possesses a number of strange single-use inventions that use xenos technology as a basis. Many are unpredictable and dangerous but Ankhet has never really cared about collateral damage if given an opportunity to use his inventions on a threat.

Methods

Xandro and Ankhet make for useful recurring villains who know how to avoid Imperial incrimination. They dabble in dangerous technologies, often sending agents with sufficient deniability to seek out xenos artefacts to secure on their behalf. Xandro and Ankhet are usually in the right place at the right time. When new xenos technology is uncovered, they dabble in the Silent Trade or insert themselves into Inquisitorial investigations to pick over the bones or steal information.

At the same time, Xandro knows how to cultivate connections and will not hesitate to invite characters to join him onboard his voidship, helping them in their adventures so he can keep a close eye on their activities and Patrons. The sooner he can convert characters from potential threats to pawns in his schemes, the better. In the case of the characters, Xandro can appear initially as a Contact or collaborator, then stab the party or their Patron in the back when it best suits his interests.

Xandro might make a play to become the characters' new Patron, using his network of spies to seek out blackmail on the characters' Patron and offer himself as a better alternative who understands their needs and provides the freedom some characters might crave. Against an Inquisitor, this is a headstrong gambit indeed, and characters who accept this deal would quickly find themselves branded a traitor, but Xandro thinks himself the centre of a cult of personality and would certainly try.

Secrets

There are many elements of Xandro’s practices which fall well within the freedoms allowed him by his Dynasty’s @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.h6Z6Ia2q5RkRUlDG]{Warrant of Trade}. Hatred for the xenos is a virtue, and Xandro’s frequent hunts and purges are eccentric at worst. However, his willingness to work with xenos technology is a proscribed activity he knows well enough to hide. Equally, his goal of wishing to lead another crusade would be seen by some as laudable, but his means and methods again betray him. Any conquest gained by means of xenos artefacts would be cursed from the outset, as such objects are not to be trusted. Nevertheless, there are Inquisitors who would embrace even this aspect of Xandro’s methods, believing it is only righteous to turn the tools of the enemy against them. Xandro himself is not so deep a thinker — anything that can bring him the victory and glory that is so obviously his right is by definition a good, even if it must be kept secret for now.

Ankhet has secrets he has kept even from his Rogue Trader accomplice. Many standard years ago, he began integrating xenos technologies into his own form, especially within his various cogitation implants. At first these additions, drawn from an ancient calculation array found in aeons-old ruins beneath the acid soils of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.B7MZBBT3bNew9N96.JournalEntryPage.59y8WFXTbwKRwiRI]{Voll}, only enhanced his abilities. As time has worn on, however, these modifications have affected his thinking deeply. During his brief maintenance cycles, he sees plans for vast planetary machinery that could alter the biosphere of entire worlds, leaving them so utterly toxic that no Human could hope to survive even a momentary exposure. Nevertheless, he feels a deep compulsion to build such a device and deploy it, despoiling a habitable world to make it suitable for beings he cannot name, and who are surely long dead. For now, he is happy to assist Xandro, as it allows him more time to refine his plans and find the materials necessary to put them into effect.

pages.name: Familiars
pages.text:
To serve the Inquisition is to know isolation on a grand scale. True knowledge of the Imperium’s foes would drive most of its citizenry to despair or madness, and many Inquisitors and their acolytes come to view most of Humanity as weak, corrupt, or hopelessly naive. It is little wonder, then, that some look beyond their fellow Humans for assistance. Though varied in origin and ability, all such non-Human servants can be referred to as Familiars.

Familiars often possess skills entirely alien to even the best-trained Human acolyte. The Adeptus Mechanicus has little understanding of xenos technology, but the Jokaero have astounding technical skills and are willing to work with almost any mechanical artefact. Psyber-familiars offer an extension of a psyker’s will and senses while avoiding the dangers of confronting another Human soul with their powers. And few can match the speed and ferocity of a cybercanid.

Familiars And Other Factions

While The Inquisition Player’s Guide focuses on the Inquisition, Familiars are not exclusive to them. Anyone with enough wealth or influence may acquire and bond with a Familiar; Inquisitors merely have enough of both and the authority to avoid awkward questions towards the more exotic Familiars they employ. The Adeptus Arbites and bounty hunters often use @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-actors.Actor.mVvzTcb8LJKDroT7]{cyber-mastiffs}, Tech-Priests are rarely without a @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-actors.Actor.Y6oJff3F4qo2Xhlx]{Servo-skull}, and even certain Chapters of the legendary Space Marines train fierce beasts to serve as companions. However, remember that some Familiars would be illegal to own in certain parts of the Imperium — particularly xenos species. Not many have the clout or influence to bend the rules like an Inquisitor.

pages.name: Familiar Rules
pages.text:
The following rules of Communication, Obedience, Instincts, Upkeep, and Advancement apply to all Familiars. In this section, we also cover rules for using Familiars in and out of Combat and acquiring one.

Communication

Except for Mechanicus constructs, Familiars do not communicate in Human language. Most of them possess the equivalent of animal intelligence, communicating basic needs and ideas (‘need food’, ‘follow me’, ‘I smell enemies nearby’, and similar concepts) instead through body language and sound. Likewise, a Familiar’s Master communicates through spoken commands and specialised gestures. Due to the time spent bonding with their Familiar, a Master explicitly understands what a Familiar might be trying to communicate, and vice versa. Anyone else must pass a Difficult (−10) Rapport (Animals) Test to decipher what either is saying to the other. Particularly security-conscious operatives may train Familiars to communicate in deliberately misleading ways, such that an onlooker suffers further penalties to the Test.

Obedience

Familiars are most effective when acting under their Master’s orders and perform poorly when acting on their own initiative. When a Familiar acts without orders or circumstances require it to be ordered by someone other than their Master, all relevant rolls are made with Disadvantage. This includes orders to attack unless they are in keeping with the Familiar’s Instincts.

Instincts

Without orders, a Familiar defaults to its Instincts. Instincts represent a creature’s natural inclinations, training, or a set of contingency protocols to engage in the absence of orders. There are two types; Combat Instincts (what role they serve in combat); and Preservation Instincts (how likely they are to run when damaged). Familiars begin with the Instincts described in their Bestiary entries. Instincts can be changed with the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.r6clx5uYnIpkdaRq.JournalEntryPage.z9PTik4AMrYlbVhR#familiar-training]{Familiar Training} Endeavour. A Familiar’s base Instincts are difficult to overcome, so the Familiar Training Endeavour can only modify one Instinct at a time.

Upkeep

Familiars need food, shelter, and regular training to remain effective. Rarer Familiars need augmetic maintenance, and some may have even stranger requirements. Each Familiar has an Upkeep cost, representing the minimum cost in Solars that must be spent to prevent their Attributes and Skills from deteriorating from malnutrition or neglect. The base Upkeep cost depends on the Master’s @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.QrGsY2UZDirxvDaB.JournalEntryPage.EH0TNUOsnWKHhwn9#payment]{Pay Grade}, the Familiar’s Size, and the number of purchased Talents. The base Upkeep Cost of a new, Average Sized Familiar is 10% of its Master’s Pay Grade. Each Talent purchased for a Familiar increases the Upkeep Cost by 4 Solars. The @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-tables.RollTable.CzOVN4IYgu7cMuAR]{Familiar Size} Table modifies all costs associated with the Familiar. Therefore, a Small Size Familiar would have a base cost of 5% of the Master’s Pay Grade, and each Talent would increase the Upkeep Cost by 2 Solars. Miserly or cruel characters may elect to spend less than the Upkeep Cost of their Familiar, but this comes with consequences. Every week, the Familiar must make a Challenging (+0) Fortitude Test or become Fatigued (Minor) until the full Upkeep Cost is paid. Failing this Test twice in a row causes the Familiar to become Fatigued (Major). Failing the Test a third time, it dies or is otherwise removed from the character’s service.

Advancement

When training a Familiar, the Master must work just as hard to ensure the bonds of trust and communication remain strong. Improving a Familiar’s Characteristics and Skills is therefore done primarily by spending XP from their Master’s pool. At the GM’s discretion, a Familiar may be awarded XP if its Master used them particularly creatively. Use the rules for @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.uJURMn2glWHhjqJk.JournalEntryPage.Dqrpb0F6t5gayyXE]{Character Advancement}. A Familiar’s maximum Characteristics and Skill levels are different from Humans and may also differ between @UUID[.YTjT0gYfJiYRSTIZ]{Familiars}. Familiars also have access to a special list of @UUID[.Vil8B54FxAl0jFcZ#familiar-talents]{Talents} that can be purchased with Master’s XP or their own (and additional Solars to cover training and materials). The Master can also upgrade a Familar to a Cyber- or Psyber-Familiar, which incurs an additional cost. A Familiar cannot be both a Cyber- or Psyber-Familiar; making this upgrade will alter them forever.

pages.name: Familiars in Combat
pages.text:
’I have people for information gathering, armaments, and whatnot, but when I finally make my move, it’s always just me and my two Cyberhounds. Never trust someone with free will and a gun at your back.’

— Jeremus Wrax, Hive Oberyl bounty hunter

Many Familiars are trained or augmented to assist their Master in combat. Hired help and allies are intelligent and independent enough to understand an Inquisitor’s plan of attack and execute their part without supervision, but Familiars lack such autonomy. The following new rules apply when using Familiars in combat:

  • Familiars with Combat Instincts do not suffer Disadvantages to Tests in combat so long as they are in keeping with those Instincts. A Familiar with Melee Instincts using a ranged attack still takes the penalty, for example.

  • A character with a Familiar must spend their Move or Action in a Turn to order their Familiar. The Familiar moves and acts on its turn in the initiative order.

  • A Familiar cannot take more than a single Move and Action in a Round unless special Abilities or psychic powers compel them.

  • Familiars are assumed to follow close to their Master unless ordered otherwise. An avian Familiar might perch on their Master’s shoulder until ordered to fly overhead and watch for threats, for example.

pages.name: Familiars Outside Combat
pages.text:
Not all Familiars are made for fighting. A Servo-Skull might possess vast data archives for quick reference in the field instead of weaponry. They all augment their Master’s capabilities in some manner.

  • Familiars with an appropriate Skill can @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf.JournalEntryPage.EwKNNdQ5EYayCPdA#getting-help]{Help} their Master on Tests. This includes Opposed (non-combat) and Extended Tests. Unless they have a Talent saying otherwise, Familiars cannot Help on attack rolls or Tests to activate psychic powers. As the Character with the highest relevant Skill makes the Test, this may result in the Master helping the Familiar.

  • At the GM’s discretion, a Familiar may provide benefits in other relevant situations. An Aeldari might be impressed with a Character who has managed to tame a particularly wilful Psyber-Familiar and be more inclined to hear them out, for example.

pages.name: Acquiring A Familiar
pages.text:
Obtaining a Familiar is a challenge; what markets the Imperium allows are carefully controlled by the Administratum and various guilds, and the most suitable creatures and machines are deliberately more expensive than most citizens could ever afford. It also takes time and effort to earn its trust and loyalty, never mind training it to the point where it becomes a workable asset.

A fully trained Familiar, ready for service, is, therefore, a significant investment in terms of both Solars and XP. Purchasing the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-items.Item.bKmzN9rjDaOIL7Uo]{Familiar Bonded} Talent allows you to own and command a Familiar; The Familiar itself must still be bought with Solars. Three levels of access may be purchased with the Talent. A Familiar may also be upgraded to a Cyber- or Psyber-Familiar, as long as the Master meets the requirements and can afford it.

Characters cannot own more Familiars than their Fellowship Bonus (FelB). In practice, very few operatives keep more than one or two Familiars; it is hard enough to feed oneself in the Imperium, let alone several dependents.

pages.name: Training A Familiar
pages.text:
With time and proper care, a Familiar can become a formidable creature in its own right, excelling in its ordained role. Though they require a great deal of training, they repay their Master’s efforts with unquestionable loyalty, dedication, and genuine friendship; a rare commodity in the 41st Millennium.

The Price Of Loyalty

Newly purchased Familiars are assumed to be previously trained to follow and obey their Master and can immediately begin to play alongside them. The Master must take charge of all further training. A Character with one or more Familiars must undertake the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.r6clx5uYnIpkdaRq.JournalEntryPage.z9PTik4AMrYlbVhR#familiar-training]{Familiar Training} Endeavour at least once between every two missions. Neglecting training risks a Familiar failing at a critical moment; if left too long, a −10 penalty is applied to all of the Familiar’s Tests, as it takes too long to register a command, hesitates, malfunctions, or simply refuses to listen.

Familiar Talents

Although Familiars tend to favour a specific role, their Master can further tailor the niche they fill with additional training. The following Talents can only be purchased for Familiars. It costs 100 XP (of the Master’s or the Familiar’s combined XP) to gain a new Talent, following the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.J8NVn5iNgM57cKmw.JournalEntryPage.ZoyVpQ2Wtbz5JA3x]{same rules} for player characters.

General Familiar Talents

Core Talents

Familiars may purchase the following listed @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.J8NVn5iNgM57cKmw.JournalEntryPage.ZoyVpQ2Wtbz5JA3x]{Talents} from Imperium Maledictum, with the same functions and requirements outlined there. pages.name: Training A Cyber-Familiar
pages.text:
Upgrading an existing Familiar to a Cyber-Familiar is a costly and gruelling process for both Familiar and Master. The Adeptus Mechanicus dislikes granting the blessings of the Omnissiah to those without proper faith in the Machine God but accepts that it is necessary to maintain the Imperium’s manufacturing and military capabilities. Providing augmetics to Familiars, less worthy again than Imperial citizens, is often viewed as a waste of a Tech-Priest’s skills and resources; as the creatures lack the proper comprehension to appreciate these gifts of steel fully, and their remaining organic components are the cause of inefficiency and aberrant behaviours and emotions. Nevertheless, demands from the wealthy and influential persist; perhaps they want to enhance existing pets or allow a valued companion to continue serving them despite critical injuries. And so the Adeptus Mechanicus charge disproportionately high fees for their service.

The procedure removes or replaces almost all of a Familiar’s organic components. Most of the brain is retained to preserve the Familiar’s behaviour, abilities, and personality and avoid the blasphemy of creating an Abominable Intelligence. Their circulatory system may be a template for a new transport system, pumping fuel to the machine and nutrients to the remaining organics. Their crude sensory organs can be replaced with blessed pict-lenses and augurs. Nerves are interfaced with cogitators grafted to the brain and a suite of pistons, micro-servos, and gyro stabilisers, allowing the creature the same or even greater range of movement than muscle and bone.

To upgrade an existing Familiar to a Cyber-Familiar, a Character must first have the required level of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-items.Item.bKmzN9rjDaOIL7Uo]{Familiar Bonded} Talent. The Master must pay Solars equal to the Familiar’s base cost for the procedure. Then make the following changes:

  • The Familiar gains 1 point of Armour. Toughness maximum increases by +20. Toughness increases by +5. The Master chooses a separate Characteristic to increase by +5.

  • The Familiar gains 1 advance in the following Skills (or Specialisations, if they already have the Skill): Fortitude (Endurance), Tech (Augmetics).

Note: These do not count towards the usual limit of the Familiar’s Toughness Bonus (TghB). Further Augmetic Replacements can be purchased now or later, counted against the usual limit.

  • Damage and Critical Wounds to the Cyber-Familiar’s augmetic locations are treated with Tech (Engineering) instead of Medicae. See @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.wqlquQ8Njtd5fb4Y.JournalEntryPage.jsw5d0omkWXaurDM#augmetic-replacements]{Imperium Maledictum} for full details on repairing augmetics.

pages.name: Training A Psyber-Familiar
pages.text:
Familiars have extremely streamlined souls compared to the galaxy’s sentient races; desire, betrayal, and all the other complex emotions that form the tides and currents of the Warp are mostly absent from such creatures. As such, few Familiars have more than the barest flicker of soul presence in the Immaterium. That connection, weak though it is, can be strengthened and made useful in service to the Imperium.

Psykers with wealth and connections may opt to turn their Familiar into a Psyber-Familiar. It is difficult to find any Tech-Priest with the knowledge required to perform the procedure, and harder still to gather the necessary resources. The Familiar receives extensive brain surgery and augmetic implants of inscrutable function, along with gruelling hypno-training and nerve stimulation to develop the neural pathways allowing a greater sense of the Warp and the souls of living things. If the procedure succeeds, both Familiar and Master must spend a great deal of time in meditative training to link their souls; in so doing, the abstract bonds of loyalty, love, and duty between Master and Familiar transform into authentic, tangible things.

A Psyker and Psyber-Familiar confer the following advantages to each other:

  • The Master’s @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.3mzwixuzgerGUpu1.JournalEntryPage.buydA5mPJln97Qk5]{Warp Threshold} is increased by the Psyber-Familiar’s Willpower bonus (WilB).

  • Each can sense the location and health status of the other (Their current Wounds and Conditions, for example) over any distance. Within Long Range, this is a free action. Over longer distances, a Challenging (+0) Willpower (Psychic Mastery) Test is required, increasing the Difficulty depending on the distance. Finding your Psyber-Familiar anywhere in a hab-block might be Challenging (+0), while pinpointing it within a whole hive city would be Difficult (−10), Hard (−20) within the scope of a continent, and so on. Further training and Talents can develop the psychic bond even further, allowing the Master to look through their Familiar’s eyes or extend the range of the Master’s psychic powers, and more.

To upgrade an existing Familiar to a Psyber-Familiar, a Character must first have the required @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-items.Item.bKmzN9rjDaOIL7Uo]{Familiar Bonded} Talent. The Master must pay Solars equal to the Familiar’s base cost for the procedure. Then make the following changes to the Familiar’s statistics:

  • Willpower maximum increases by +20. Willpower increases by +5. The Master chooses another Characteristic to increase by +5.

  • The Familiar gains 1 Advance in the following Skills (or Specialisations, if they already have the Skill): Awareness (Psyniscience), Discipline (Psychic), and Psychic Mastery.

  • Wounds increase by their Master’s Willpower Bonus.

Psyber-Familiar Talents

These Talents can only be purchased by Psyber-Familiars. It costs 100 XP (of the Master’s or the Familiar’s combined XP) to gain a new @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.J8NVn5iNgM57cKmw.JournalEntryPage.ZoyVpQ2Wtbz5JA3x]{Talent}, following the same rules for player characters.

pages.name: Creating A Familiar
pages.text:
The galaxy contains an almost infinite variety of creatures and constructs that might make suitable Familiars, and these are often further tailored mechanically and genetically to fit their Master’s precise needs. A player may simply choose a premade Familiar to accompany their character (from the @UUID[.CXjCudhmpd5uT0Yj]{Familiar Bestiary}), some of which have special Traits and higher costs, or create their own if they cannot find one that best suits their character’s needs or desires.

To create a Familiar, follow these steps. Choosing from the associated Tables or roll to generate their new Familiar’s features and traits randomly (note that rolling randomly still affects the Familiar’s cost in some places).

  1. A Familiar’s base Cost is 10,000 Solars, and their base Upkeep cost is 10% of their Master’s Pay Grade.

  2. Determine Familiar’s Size (See @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-tables.RollTable.CzOVN4IYgu7cMuAR]{Familiar Size} Table). Note the Cost Multiplier, and apply it to the initial cost of the Familiar.

  3. A Familiar’s Characteristics all start at 5. Increase the Familiar’s Characteristics as desired, using a pool of 200 points. Unless modified by Familiar Size, the maximum for any Characteristic is 50.

  4. Determine Familiar’s Combat and Preservation Instincts (See Familiar Instincts Table).

  5. Determine Familiar’s Mobility (See Familiar Mobility Table).

  6. Choose 5 Skills to gain 1 Advance each, and give one of them a @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.J8NVn5iNgM57cKmw.JournalEntryPage.2MqLlcSMDCxkumCk#specialisations]{Skill Specialisation}.

  7. Add 2 @UUID[.Vil8B54FxAl0jFcZ#familiar-talents]{Familiar Talents}.

  8. Add @UUID[.1KVRCsdRBsWAbvN9]{Cyber-} or @UUID[.aul6tv8Zh6mX52Ly]{Psyber-} template, if desired. This will further increase the base cost, including additional Talents or Augmetics.

  9. If the Familiar is a Cyber-Familiar, its type is Construct. Otherwise, its type is Beast.

  10. Derive Wounds (based on the Wounds column in the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-tables.RollTable.CzOVN4IYgu7cMuAR]{Familiar Size} Table), Critical Wounds (equal to their Toughness Bonus), Encumbrance (Strength Bonus + Toughness Bonus) and Initiative (their Perception Bonus + Agility Bonus).

  11. Determine Quirks (See @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-tables.RollTable.j7xwtmxepVD5r597]{Familiar Quirk} Table) and Name the Familiar.

Additional Notes (unless otherwise stated):

  • A Familiar's Role is Troop.

  • Familiars have no Fate.

  • Familiars have no Handedness.

  • Familiars have a Resolve equal to their Master’s (if their Master is an NPC).

  • Familiars begin with no Armour unless an effect grants them any during creation.

  • Familiars don’t naturally have a Faction but belong to their Master’s Faction by extension.

  • All Familiars have an Unarmed Attack (Melee (Brawling), 0 + StrB Damage. @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.wqlquQ8Njtd5fb4Y.JournalEntryPage.wsM53RDPPrqwS3Te#ineffective]{Ineffective}).

An alternative to creating a Familiar from scratch, players can choose from a wide selection of creatures within the Familiar Bestiary. Among them are some of the galaxy’s most iconic creatures, from Cyber-Mastifs to Psyber-Eaglers or even the enigmatic Jokaero.

pages.name: Patrons of the Inquisition
pages.text:
‘Your objections are irrelevant; I am an Inquisitor, and I answer to none save the Emperor of Mankind. Regarding my methods, He seems content to remain silent.’

— Inquisitor [NAMES REDACTED, SEE CASE ID #3421-G3/Delta-48F3 ‘Vitezovich’]

Perhaps alone among the Imperium’s institutions, the Inquisition values individuality in its operatives. The one thing that truly unites them is their duty to protect the Imperium from its many foes. Each Inquisitor is largely free to perform that duty however they see fit, and their authority to do so is second only to the Emperor Himself. They know far more about their enemies’ true natures than most citizens are ever permitted, and they carry the terrible burden of knowing that in a galaxy of unending nightmares, there are few means that cannot be justified.

This chapter expands on @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.QrGsY2UZDirxvDaB]{Creating a Patron}, providing far more options for Inquisitorial Patrons. It provides rules for creating Patrons drawn from each of the Ordos Majoris, with either Puritan or Radical philosophies.

You are not required to adhere only to this book; while millennia of tradition and dogma carry tremendous weight in all Imperial institutions, Inquisitors are not bound by the considerations of their lessers. Inquisitors come from all backgrounds, and they take the lessons they learned in their old lives with them. If you desire a Patron who was a commissar before earning her Inquisitorial seal, you are free to take Boons or Liabilities from the Astra Militarum Faction, for example. Similarly, the options listed here need not be exclusive to the Inquisition. The @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-items.Item.S56anxusJpE26v03]{Arms of the Alien} Boon, for example, would equally suit a @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.QrGsY2UZDirxvDaB.JournalEntryPage.Nu2YQ7B987wE76SL#rogue-trader-dynasty]{Rogue Trader} or @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.QrGsY2UZDirxvDaB.JournalEntryPage.Nu2YQ7B987wE76SL#infractionist]{Infractionist} Patron dealing in bartered @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-items.Item.7rzrR5VhG6YQyaAY]{Splinter Rifles} and other alien weaponry. Any of the Patron options in current and future books may make more sense for the particular Inquisitor you have in mind for your game. An Inquisitor’s near-limitless authority allows them to acquire almost any benefit (or drawback) for their operatives.

The module provides a separate sheet for Inquisition Patrons. This can be accessed via the Sheet Configuration menu at the top of any Patron sheet.

PATRON CREATION SUMMARY

Creating an Inquisitor Patron follows a similar process to the one outlined in @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.QrGsY2UZDirxvDaB]{Creating a Patron}, with a few minor changes. The following process offers an alternative to using the Ordo Hereticus and Ordo Xenos Faction Options presented in Imperium Maledictum.

If you have already created an Inquisitorial Patron and wish to make use of some of the options found in this book, you should feel free to do so. In justifying any changes, consider how the Patron may have changed and grown over time, and what information they may have withheld from their servants.

1) FACTION

Choose one of the Major Ordo Factions for your Inquisitor Patron to belong to: @UUID[.8VBBA2YizW1qXO0A]{Hereticus}, @UUID[.UHsOV7Fx69tGx7Af]{Malleus}, @UUID[.ii5T5A2xNvL3NEdQ]{Xenos}.

2) PHILOSOHPY

Choosing either Radical or Puritan.

Then, based on your choice, you may choose an @UUID[.lFT1A8eGYjmaOne2]{Inquisition Philosophy} from those available. Not every Inquisitor adheres to these schools of thought, but they each carry a certain weight within the organisation. These individual philosophies offer no mechanical benefit, but choosing and discussing one with your GM can bring the group to a consensus on what aspects of the Inquisition you wish your campaign to explore. These philosophies and more are discussed in greater detail within the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.brh2O5CexxurRbM7.JournalEntryPage.DvP1i46KYTgkMN0W]{Inquisition GM's Guide}.

3) DEMEANOR

Humanity is endlessly diverse, and the Inquisition encourages individuality in its members, meaning even two Puritans of the same Ordo will have markedly different personalities. Roll or choose an entry in the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-tables.RollTable.gPwiEavBh82AoryT]{Patron Demeanour Table}.

4) BOONS

All Inquisitor Patrons possess the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.3M9o35qxoxiQRzP5]{Limitless Authority} Boon, and each Ordo grants a chosen Puritan or Radical Philosophy Boon, depending on your prior Philosophy choice. Additionally, players can choose (or randomly determine) up to two more Boons for their Patron. Selecting Boons from their corresponding Duty’s Boons and Liabilities Table is a good place to start, but any Boon from @UUID[.6XDRyZRTgmE04jQq]{this book} or from @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.QrGsY2UZDirxvDaB.JournalEntryPage.JiJ2Z5aXJoIhESRX]{Imperium Maledictum} is available. Be aware that the GM will secretly apply a Liability for every Boon chosen.

5) LIABILITIES

The GM secretly chooses one Liability for each Boon the Patron has. Like Boons, selecting from their Duty’s Boons and Liabilities Table is a great place to start, but any Liability in @UUID[.bG321fa56zET2lae]{this book} or from @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.QrGsY2UZDirxvDaB.JournalEntryPage.z2s8dXrvTS7rx1J4]{Imperium Maledictum} is available to them.

6) BACKGROUND AND INFLUENCE

Each Inquisitor Patron has +2 Influence with the Inquisition.

Name your Patron (You can use the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.uJURMn2glWHhjqJk.JournalEntryPage.PwG5oioCaLgyqLWX#name]{Name Table}).

Your Patron offers a Standard @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.QrGsY2UZDirxvDaB.JournalEntryPage.EH0TNUOsnWKHhwn9#payment]{Payment Grade} (this can be modified, depending on certain chosen Boons and Liabilities).

The Gamemaster can continue to flesh out the Patron’s character however they like, potentially using @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.uJURMn2glWHhjqJk.JournalEntryPage.PwG5oioCaLgyqLWX]{Adding Detail} and @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.uJURMn2glWHhjqJk.JournalEntryPage.jO0rmqIrT2EL3tyo]{Bringing Your Character to Life}.

Note: Any Boons and Liabilities marked with an asterisk (*) can affect your Patron’s Influence. Unless otherwise stated, each Boon and Liability can only be taken once. An Inquisitor Patron’s Motivation is replaced by their Philosophy.

pages.name: Faction: Ordo Hereticus
pages.text:
'Assume nothing - no writ no warrant, no seal, save my own - is truly valid. The heretic hides behind the titles and honours of the Imperium just as surely as they lurk among the wretched and the malcontent.'

- Inquisitor @UUID[Compendium.impmal-starter-set.actors.Actor.Oh1HWiuX3Lmk0q0l]{Aegidius Halikarn}

Your Patron belongs to the section of the Inquisition chiefly concerned with identifying and eliminating heresy. Preachers and lay citizens deviating from the Ministorum’s Imperial Creed, mutation, and witchcraft are cornerstones of the Ordo’s work, but the Imperium’s political power structures are so intertwined with its religion that ‘heresy’ can encompass almost any threat. Criminality, protests against oppression, consorting with xenos, and even genuinely pious individuals whose words or actions are politically inconvenient may fall under the gaze of the Ordo Hereticus.

Influence: Your Patron has +2 Influence with the Inquisition.

pages.name: Faction: Ordo Malleus
pages.text:
'Fear not, for the wards I've placed upon your bones will preserve your soul even if the flesh is flensed from them by the horrors duty demands you face.'

- Inquisitor Ksenia Baek

Your Patron is a member of the Ordo Malleus, the arm of the Inquisition devoted to eliminating daemonic threats. Unchecked heresy, Rogue Psykers and more may result in the warp and its terrible inhabitants spilling out into realspace, and the Ordo Malleus investigates all of these and more. Some are ruthless witch-hunters, who consider every psyker a catastrophe in waiting, while others are psykers themselves, using their powers to protect the Imperium against the daemonic. Preventing warp incursions is their primary duty, but when all else fails they alone have the authority to call upon the Grey Knights — the deadly and secretive daemon-hunting Space Marines.

pages.name: Faction: Ordo Xenos
pages.text:
'Flame, bolt, and blade - all are but tools. Your true weapon against the xenos is contempt. Let it fester in your heart, let it strengthen your will, and their wiles will not assail you.'

- Inquisitor Konstan Serranus

Your Patron belongs to the Inquisition’s alien hunters, the Ordo Xenos. Their mandate is to further the mono-domination of Humanity across the galaxy and protect the Imperium’s borders from alien threats. They investigate and catalogue xenos species, seeking to discover their weaknesses and if they can be taken advantage of for the Imperium’s gain. Ork infestations, Aeldari meddling, and insurrections fomented by the so-called diplomacy of the T’au, all fall within their purview. Puritans strive to destroy the alien and all their works without exception, while Radicals may exploit xenotech, ally with xenos temporarily, or even employ the services of alien mercenaries from time to time. When an alien threat is beyond the skills of the Inquisitor’s operatives, they can call upon Deathwatch killteams; elite xenos-hunting groups of Space Marines, hand-picked from across the Chapters of the Adeptus Astartes for their expertise in eliminating xenos threats.

Influence: Your Patron has +2 Influence with the Inquisition.

Duty Boon: Your Patron has the Duty Boon: @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.3M9o35qxoxiQRzP5]{Limitless Authority}.

pages.name: Patron Philosophies
pages.text:
There are as many opinions within the Holy Orders of the Emperor’s Inquisition as there are Inquisitors to hold them. Though their Holy Order may guide an Inquisitor’s focus, how they go about the business of protecting the Imperium varies wildly from one Inquisitor to another, informed by their own particular beliefs and principles. Some seek to burn every trace of their heretical foes to ash, while others preserve the tools of their enemies and seek to put them to better use. Some seek out heresy by casting a vast and terrifying net, watching for what unsurfaces with little regard for collateral damage. Others seek out corruption with scalpel-like precision, removing the malignancy without leaving any trace.

Nevertheless, certain common schools of thought have emerged over the millennia. Some of these philosophies have many adherents, and the actions they inspired have led to the salvation or damnation of entire worlds. Other philosophies are little more than fringe beliefs, shared in secret among the devoted, yet to fulfil their true potential.

Puritans and Radicals

Inquisitors are universally strong-willed individuals, for who else could hope to serve the Emperor in such a task as theirs? However, few can confront the horrors facing the Imperium and not be shaped by them, no matter how iron their will. New Inquisitors often hold fast to the principles they held prior to their ascension, confident that the Lex Imperialis or the doctrine of the Imperial Creed will be sufficient to guide their hand in dispensing the Emperor’s justice.

This is almost never the case. The horrors an Inquisitor must face are trying on even the most resolute soul. Coming to understand the true extent of corruption within the Imperium, the depths to which Humanity can sink, and the incomprehensible swath of alien foes that stand ready to assail every redoubt takes its toll, and most Inquisitors come to reassess their views.

Being Puritan or Radical is a broad spectrum. Some turn inwards, their faith in their chosen creed becoming an obsession that excludes any other consideration.

Such Puritan Inquisitors can become increasingly staunch and inflexible. They may not tolerate deviance, no matter how minor, and ultimately may start to see the Imperium itself as uncomfortably accepting of the heresies it supposedly rejects.

Other Inquisitors slip into more Radical mindsets, so blind to the nuances of reality that they do the Imperium few favours. They can feel driven to more extreme and questionable actions by what they see as necessity and lesser evils. They could take up the tools of the xenos and the heretic, believing they alone can resist the temptation and corruption that has claimed so many, or simply accepting that their own fall is a necessary cost that must be paid.

On a similar axis, Inquisitors at either end of this spectrum may overlook minor heresies to combat greater ones, judging the importance of their specific target over the broader missions of the Holy Orders. Others may become disillusioned with Humanity, no longer seeing people as anything other than pawns to be exploited in their private wars or putting the letter of the Imperial Lex above the people it’s supposed to serve.

Just like the player characters, consider where your Patron’s story began and how they’ll grow as the campaign progresses. Based on their experiences past, present and future, and the choices they are forced to make — many will arise because of the player’s actions — consider if they’ll take a more Puritan or Radical approach and if that might shift their philosophies.

Apart from an initial stance of Puritan or Radical, you do not need to choose a specific Philosophy right away. You can wait and see how the Patron character develops or choose once your characters have completed a few missions and have a better idea of what they want to accomplish. The Inquisitor’s actual Philosophy may even be a closely guarded secret to them alone. Below are seven of the major Inquisition Philosophies prevalent within the Macharian Sector. While prevalent, not every Inquisitor subscribes to one of these Philosophies, or indeed to any other. Most Inquisitors find their outlooks changed by the nature of their work, often in uncomfortable ways, and many may change their outlook over time. Further Philosophies — many more esoteric or evolved — are discussed in the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.brh2O5CexxurRbM7.JournalEntryPage.DvP1i46KYTgkMN0W]{Inquisition GM's Guide}. The following examples cover the Philosophies of Inquisitors characters may encounter within the Macharian Sector.

Amalathian

The Imperium’s institutions and the God-Emperor are one and the same. We must preserve both.

Atop Mount Amalath on Gathalamor, at the dawn of the 41st millennium, political, military, and religious leaders from across the galaxy renewed their oaths to the God-Emperor. This conclave, it is said, spurred Lord Solar Macharius to launch his crusade, eventually forming the sector bearing his name. Amalathians believe fervently in maintaining the status quo. The ancient institutions founded by the God-Emperor are themselves sacred, and to deviate from their laws is to question His divine plan. They seek to eliminate anything that might destabilise the Imperium’s institutions, be it an upstart political movement or infighting between organisations. Amalathians typically promote strength through unity, adherence to tradition, and resistance to change. Unsurprisingly, this tends to endear Amalathians to many of the Imperium’s hidebound Factions.

For some time, Amalathianism has been the prime philosophy of the Inquisitors in the Macharian Sector due to the need for unity in the face of the Macharian Heresies — rebuilding Imperial hierarchies as readily as purging what stood in their place. In recent years, many Inquisitors still exhort Amalthian tenets, but the dogma is a convenient guise for Inquisitors to hide their true beliefs, especially for the Radical.

Isstvanian

The most terrible threats to the Imperium beget its greatest heroes. Conflict makes us strong.

Isstvanians argue that Humanity requires conflict to grow. They take their name from the atrocities marking the start of the Horus Heresy, believing it was a catalyst for greater things; did it not, after all, weed out the Primarchs and Astartes who betrayed the Imperium? Did it not allow the Emperor’s divine Ascension to the Golden Throne? Isstvanians foster war and violence across the Imperium, ensuring the weak are sacrificed so the strong may grow stronger. An Isstvanian’s mindset may frequently land on the decision to further conflict over forging an unsteady peace, but they do not operate recklessly; their end goal is to strengthen the Imperium as a whole. Though millions may die, their trials are carefully calculated to expose weakness and corruption, that the righteous will redouble their fury and forge their souls in the battle to exterminate it.

The Macharian Sector is ripe for Isstvanian meddling. Beyond the countless cults and xenos incursions, some noble families still resent bending the knee to God-Emperor during the crusade. With a small injection of power and manipulation, they could rise as a renewed enemy, to be crushed and purged by the Imperium’s might, or expose a weakness that needs bolstering.

Recongrator

The Imperium stagnates. Corrupt pretenders rule the Macharian Sector. This must change.

Recongregators believe the Imperium’s institutions are beyond saving. They must be torn down and replaced with organisations that better serve Humanity. The so-called Macharian Recongregators specifically believe that the root cause of the Sector’s woes is the generals who succeeded Macharius upon his death, even those who remained loyal to the Imperium. Their descendants still hold positions of authority in the sector, from minor hive nobles to Sector Lord Sejanus himself, and are unfit for purpose in these dire times.

Macharian Recongregators work to undermine these rulers, destabilise their power bases, and research ancient lines of succession for any justification to depose and replace them. These actions brand them as Radicals and naturally bring them into frequent conflict with Puritan factions, especially Amalathians. There is also division within the movement between those who believe in slow, gradual reform and those who would topple the power structure and rebuild it all at once.

Monodominant

Humanity can only survive if everything that threatens it is eradicated without remit.

By turns pessimistic and bombastic, Monodominants believe that Humanity will be wiped out if any enemy is permitted to survive, and thus, every enemy must be destroyed. Monodominants are utterly uncompromising and ruthless; there is no excuse for heresy of any kind, and the only punishment is death. Precisely what constitutes heresy can vary according to personal bias and prevailing attitudes of the time, but whatever a Monodominant’s values are, they are applied strictly to the letter. The philosophy is prevalent among younger Inquisitors who believe their work has no shades of morality. They tend to be militant and likely to operate in the open, leading massacres, witch trials, and mutant purges.

Other Inquisitors are frequently accused of heresy by Monodominants, who believe that no one, not even another Inquisitor, is above suspicion. Inquisitors outside their beliefs usually find Monodominants narrowminded and lacking perspective.

Any Monodominant Inquisitor will find plentiful work in the Macharian Sector. Set at the farthest reaches of the Imperium, with so many recently conquered worlds in its borders and xenos influence reaching in from beyond — an Inquisitor could overturn any Hive City at random and find heresy abundant in one form or another. Indeed, young Inquisitors might find themselves overwhelmed and their philosophy challenged just as quickly.

Oblationist

To use the tools of the enemy is damnation. We acknowledge this; the Imperium is worth such a sacrifice.

Puritans claim that the enemy’s works bring only damnation. Oblationists, unusually for a Radical philosophy, agree; they merely consider their souls a small price to pay for the safety of the Imperium. Oblationists are extremely secretive, knowing their beliefs would be cause for execution even in the Inquisition, and operatives who somehow learn of their Patron’s beliefs are either sworn to secrecy themselves or eliminated. Being already damned, Oblationist Inquisitors are willing to employ any method to battle the darkness, swearing mighty oaths to destroy themselves before becoming that which they fight.

An Oblationist Inquisitor would have no qualms about supporting the rise of a heretical cult if they could ultimately wield it against a greater threat, especially if they expect or intend these operatives to die in their service. As such, an Oblationist’s operatives are sometimes Infractionists or outright heretics, believing they work against the Imperium. The Macharian Sector lacks neither. The recent fragmentation of the sector has given rise to many small cults and gangs, ready to be manipulated into action, even against each other.

Polypsykanna

Psychic awakening is a gift. With guidance, Humanity may transcend mortal flesh and join the Emperor in immortality.

In almost every corner of the Imperium, psykers are necessary but never wanted. The Radicals of the Polypsykana see things differently. Like it or not, they argue, Humanity is becoming a psychic species.

Humanity’s psychic potential must be carefully protected, nurtured, and explored so that when we are ready, we may transcend our physical forms and become purely psychic beings. Polypsykanans investigate and study all facets of the Warp and its interactions with consciousness. The majority join the Ordo Malleus or Hereticus, where they can find and shepherd Human psykers. Still, there are Ordo Xenos Polypsykanans who believe alien technologies may be key to Humanity’s apotheosis. The most driven seek out alliances with the Aeldari, latent witches all, to learn what they can and apply it to their studies. Most Puritans see the Polypsykana as dangerously tolerant at best and at worst, no better than the witches they purge.

Due to the Noctis Aeterna, Polypsykana Inquisitors in the Macharian Sector have access to a massive backlog of imprisoned pskyers, to recruit from or experiment on, to further their research. Too many Black Ships have been lost to the Warp or are significantly late to pick up their tithe; certainly, system officials wouldn’t mind if a trusted Inquisitor took some off their hands.

Thorian

The God-Emperor will walk among us again. We must find the perfect vessel for His Divine Will to inhabit.

The Thorian philosophy stands upon two pillars of belief. First, the God-Emperor was long ago shorn from realspace and now travels the Imperium in spirit, where he grants shards of His Divine Will upon chosen citizens, those who may exhibit saintly or psychic blessings for the good of the Imperium. Secondly, one day He will find a vessel capable of containing all of His might and return to us, renew the Imperium, and lead Humanity on a new galactic conquest.

The Thorian’s goal is to seek out such a vessel or construct one in His stead to manifest this new age of the Imperium faster. Their opponents claim that if the God-Emperor resurrects in such a way, it would cause a civil war across the Imperium and tear the Imperial Faith apart, not to mention a host of other unknowns it would bring to bear, such as the continued function of the Astronomicon, or what would happen to the entity sat upon the Golden Throne. In the Macharian Sector, Thorians have countless worlds to explore, host to purported miracles or lost Imperium or xenos technologies that could all aid their research. The sector is a primed stage for the God-Emperor’s return, rife with turmoil, ready to be led into a new era, and far from Terra’s oversight.

Not every Boon is suitable for any one Patron, depending on their Puritan or Radical stance and what @UUID[.lFT1A8eGYjmaOne2]{Philosophy} they believe in. Your group should consider the corresponding Boons and Liabilities Tables for a base set of options. Some Boons award Influence with a Faction and a factional effect during play, representing alliances your Patron has made through their illustrious (or infamous) career. Though not all Boons award Influence in this way, the Gamemaster might like to use these Boons as inspiration for modifying the Patron’s future Influence gains.

pages.name: Influence
pages.text:
Your Patron is one of the most powerful people in the Imperium, and much of their power is represented by their connections to leaders and characters within other Imperium Factions and organisations. No one can deny them, by the law of the Emperor Himself, but that won’t stop them from slowing down requests or throwing a combi-tool into the works to satisfy their own secret vendetta. Conversely, those in thrall to your Inquisitor’s influence may be eager to provide service and open up all doors within their organisation to you.

All Inquisition Patrons begin with +2 Influence and may have gained or lost some Influence depending on what Boons and Liabilities they acquired during creation. Your characters will be aware of your Patron’s positive Influence when you start the game, but their Patron’s Influence can change and is secretly tracked thereafter by the GM. Any negative Influence your Patron has is unknown to the players, but it can be revealed during your missions depending on who they interact with and what information they can gather. More information about Background and Influence is detailed in @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.QrGsY2UZDirxvDaB.JournalEntryPage.Nu2YQ7B987wE76SL]{Imperium Maledictum}.

Remember that your character’s Influence is different from your Patrons, where they may turn you away or treat you as their enemy, your Patron’s Influence may be more favourable, and vice-versa.

But my Authority is Limitless!

You might find yourself asking why, if an Inquisitor’s authority is limitless, Influence even matters. Surely all that needs to happen is a demand be made, and compliance must surely follow? Certain Inquisitors may even believe this to be true.

To Inquisitor Patrons, Influence is not so literal as it is for other members of the Adeptus Terra. A high Influence with one faction could be forged by genuine respect or even enrapturing fear bred from their propagandised authority. Similarly, a negative level of Influence may be borne by a group’s hatred towards the Inquisition, as much as they might slow a request by naturally tripping over their protocols.

pages.name: Roleplaying Inquisitors
pages.text:
Inquisitors see the Imperium from an incomparable vantage, burdened with unique scope, power, and freedom of thought. Their duty is to no system, sector, or segmentum, but to the God-Emperor’s domain as a whole. They serve no master save Him on Terra. Their freedom to interpret their duty places them beyond the hold of the Lex Imperialis and Imperial Creed, holding doubts and philosophies that any ordinary citizen would be condemned for. These few souls, who know the true breadth of horrors that threaten to choke the Imperium, bear a duty to become horrors themselves, for in the salvation of the Imperium, there is no deed beyond their limits, no cost counted in Human lives that is deemed too high. Billions of souls have been condemned on the orders of the Inquisition, for innocence is never enough for a soul to be spared.

In their scope and jurisdiction, the only souls of equal standing to an Inquisitor are others of their creed. Inquisitors primarily work alone, typically only coming together to face the direst threats. To the citizens of the Imperium, Inquisitors are so far removed from their everyday lives that they are made near-mythic through their distance and holy duties — terrors lurking in the darkness to some, little more than tall tales to most. Inquisitors act with the full sanction and authority of the God-Emperor; they are His eyes in the darkest corners of the Imperium and His instrument of justice and punishment. To the people of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.B7MZBBT3bNew9N96.JournalEntryPage.VeiDfnkV55kTAkRw]{Kallastin}, a world that felt the sting of their presence in the Macharian Heresy, Inquisitors are remembered as the lurking death of the apostate, the God-Emperor’s wrath and tyranny manifest.

This chapter provides advice and inspiration for GMs portraying Inquisitor Patrons in their games. How to build their mythology and relationships with their acolyte characters and portray them as the utterly terrifying and world-shaking characters they truly are. Additionally, there is mechanical advice about setting up briefings and debriefings with your players' characters, how they should they be treated in moments of loyalty and betrayal, and how GMs and players alike should handle the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.b06xyMjo4E4cYc40]{Inquisitor’s Rosette} as a defining piece of equipment.

Macharian Inquisitors

This Chapter contain a roster of sample Inquisitor Patrons, who are also the leading personalities of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.FNEW8e33IisZh27W]{Chapter V: The Heresies Macharia }. These can be used as pre-made Patrons during character creation or as allied or opposed characters in your campaigns. Take note of their secrets, but do not share them with your players. Note each one’s Future Boons & Liabilities Table, which suggests additional upgrades and downgrades that can affect players and Patrons alike when they reach story milestones.

pages.name: Duty & Ambition
pages.text:
Inquisitors are individualistic people with powerful personalities that defy true categorisation. Those who share the same Ordo should not be painted with the same broad brush. Two major and often opposing principles guide an Inquisitor’s motivations. First, the duties demanded of them by the Holy Orders. Second, by the ambition of their philosophy. Through these principles combined, each Inquisitor forms their definitive and personal understanding of how best to serve and preserve the Imperium.

The Inquisitor’s Ordo defines their principal area of investigation — what each Inquisitor is actively searching for. However, this is often simply a starting point. If an Ordo Hereticus Inquisitor is investigating a Chaos-worshipping cult revealed to be under the influence of xenos corruption, they must still purge this cult. They cannot simply hand the investigation over to an Ordo Xenos Inquisitor and move on just because the threat does not match their Ordo’s charge. They must tackle the threat head-on, but they are more likely to reach out to Ordo Xenos operatives for advice and support.

Their philosophical faction will influence their methods and desired outcomes — but not so far as to conflict with their ultimate duty of serving and protecting the Imperium. Puritans may demand their acolytes publicly uphold their faith during operations, while Radicals often hide behind masks of false Puritan philosophies to continue their ancillary works undisturbed. Characters serving an @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.brh2O5CexxurRbM7.JournalEntryPage.R7LueEsDUhrSYHNn]{Amalathian} Inquisitor might be instructed to strike down any heretical collaborators within the Adeptus Terra they come upon or use them to root out further heresies. Meanwhile, those serving a Radical @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.brh2O5CexxurRbM7.JournalEntryPage.s88kgPSDiogPL4aB]{Xanthite} Inquisitor might be granted powerful Warp-tainted weaponry to purge their opposition effectively while simultaneously being expected to keep such technologies secret.

Consider how the aspects of Ordo and Philosophy are presented between yourself as the GM and your players characters. For characters, understanding their Ordo’s duties should be relatively straightforward. Engaged in activities related to mission-specific objectives and what threats and situations they are likely to encounter. At the same time, their Patron’s Philosophy should initially be shrouded in mystery, one gradually peeled away as missions occur and the Inquisitor grows to trust their acolytes.

Plans Within Plans

Each Inquisitor has a range of agents and resources, some may operate with only a tight circle of agents and singular cells, while others might have hundreds or thousands of operatives at their disposal. Yet the time Inquisitors can spend with their various agents, especially in person, is often at a premium. Even if the Inquisitor had a direct hand in an acolyte’s recruitment, they may rarely meet in person, receiving instead various missives or orders passed through their chain of command. They are more likely to be granted time with one of the Inquisitor’s Interrogators or high-ranking members of their retinue.

The reason for this is straightforward: most Inquisitors are mired in hundreds of different heretical plots and investigations at any given time. Though any cell’s mission is crucial to their plans, the characters are only one of possibly thousands of cells across the sector, each operating independently and often compartmentalised for years to decades at a time.

Meeting with their Inquisitor should often be a reverent moment. The characters are confronted with one of the sector's most powerful entities, someone thought to be imbued with the God-Emperor’s will. They will never meet anyone more influential for the rest of their comparatively infinitesimal lives.

That said, if their Patron is physically present before them, it means the characters have often done something tremendously wrong or exceptionally right. They should feel the weight of this moment appropriately and ensure the Inquisitor’s actions reflect their nigh-infinite power. If displeased, they may be punished before their comrades, or rewarded with authority and equipment that cannot be found outside the Inquisition.

How much an Inquisitor leads the characters' cell after that point is up to you as the GM. The Inquisitor’s presence should only be maintained when the stakes are appropriately high. Characters should always feel on edge when around their Patron. They are powerful, influential, and ostensibly on the characters' side. Still, it is often only a matter of time before an Inquisitor’s suspicions turn on their servants or, if pleased, the Inquisitor themselves become so radical or corrupt that the characters should grow suspicious of them.

Other Cells & Operatives

When an Inquisitor must ensure a mission succeeds, they can deploy more than one cell of acolytes to the same area. Other Inquisitorial acolytes operating nearby are neither a boon nor a liability to the characters; they are another narrative force you can include as the GM to add an extra twist to the story

Competing cells may set the bar high, effectively at odds for the Inquisitor’s favour; the Patron may see healthy competition as a means to drive the effectiveness of both teams. Rivalries are likely, and for players, it opens another avenue to their roleplay experience. On the other hand, the characters could be sent to clean up another cell’s blunders, presenting mistakes the players' cell should avoid or other avenues for investigation they might have missed earlier.

For redundancy’s sake, the other cell can also be a source of replacement characters should one of the players' characters die in the line of duty — which is never outside the realm of possibilities given the enemies the Inquisition regularly faces.

Characters might encounter a cell or acolytes of another Inquisitor. In most cases, they should be immediately wary of these other acolytes, being a group just as dangerous or more capable than themselves. It is rare for more than one Inquisitor to happen upon the same target of investigation; canny characters should take the initiative to figure out why they are here. The other cell might have different and conflicting goals or exploit the investigation to spy on the characters and, by extension, their Patron’s organisation.

Influence

When your characters meet another Inquisitor or their acolytes in the field, you may give them their own level of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf.JournalEntryPage.qxkAEAcB9xAl56Xa]{Influence} to represent levels of trust and favours earned between cells or Patrons.

If you need a starting point, consider using the same value as the characters' Influence with the Inquisition or that Inquisitor’s Ordo, representing what they might have heard about the characters' reputation. From there, Influence can degrade or improve independently as if the Inquisitor were their own Faction. But make it clear to your players that there is still a positive and negative link. Reaching an Honoured level of Influence with an Ordo Xenos Inquisitor could improve their standing with the Ordo as a whole, but the same goes for becoming Vilified or Hunted.

Between Inquisitors

Inquisitors meeting in the field should be a significant moment in any campaign, akin to an unstoppable force meeting an immovable object. Even a meeting between cells can be a turning point in the narrative — will these new NPCs present themselves as an aid or hindrance to the characters? Given the Inquisition’s penchant for deception, the characters may not know they have a powerful new opposition until it is too late.

Despite appearances, characters should be wary of this meeting of giants occurring; the Imperium and its heresies are so vast that encountering another Inquisitor’s cell or Inquisitor themselves is often no mere coincidence. It could mean that both Inquisitors are after the same target or ‘prize’, which could result in some level of collaboration. But it is just as likely that Inquisitors stand at opposite ends of the Radical-Puritan spectrum or behind competing philosophies. As utterly intractable characters, neither Inquisitor would back down without bringing their influence to bear against the other — either the surmounting threat of violence or underhanded harm against the other. In this, they will need the aid of trusted acolytes to get their hands dirty and provide a modicum of plausible deniability

These revolving philosophical struggles can be a campaign’s backdrop or central point of conflict. Some Inquisitors are so directly opposed to one another’s aims that sabotaging the work of another Inquisitor may appear more vital to an Inquisitor than their duties to their Ordo. Here, characters spend time surveilling opposing cells of acolytes between acts of counter-espionage to protect themselves and their Patron, waiting to pull the trigger only until they uncover damnable proof of the enemy Inquisitor’s heretical activities (or defending the Radical actions of their own). This can happen behind the scenes of more ‘regular’ Inquisitorial investigations, perhaps to string together a series of disparate one-shot adventures or missions.

In extreme cases, the active hunting of an enemy Inquisitor can be the entire focus of a campaign. Every other Imperial organisation meticulously purges the records of heresy in their ranks from archiviums and datavaults; the Inquisition strives to maintain the ‘true’ record of heresy across the Imperium, even among their own ranks. Where sufficient evidence is presented, an alleged heretical Inquisitor may be declared Excommunicate Traitoris by their peers, a condemnation that rallies other Inquisitors to pursue and destroy this rogue and their agents. For Inquisitors who take on this responsibility out of piety, philosophical opposition to the condemned, or realising an opportunity for personal gain, their acolytes assume the role of hunting hounds.

pages.name: Rosettes
pages.text:
An Inquisitorial Rosette is a badge of holy office, wielded by Inquisitors and their agents to bypass the order of common, lesser souls and respected by all factions, institutes and houses of the Imperium. The construction and function of Rosettes are as varied as the Inquisitors who bear them, and carry the classified attributes of their masters’ power and duties. Some carry genetically encoded details of an Inquisitor’s identity and prove they operate with the Throne of Terra’s authority

Rosettes are rarely used in dealings with the common populace of Imperial worlds. To flaunt Inquisitorial authority is to draw attention, elicit fear, and demand absolute acquiescence. Rosettes see sparing use in ground-level investigations, for the sight of one will often sow word of the Inquisition’s presence, spreading unease through a local populace and alerting those who would prefer their heretical deeds remained in the shadow. In the rare moments when a Rosette is bared in this manner of investigation, it is understood by those who view it as a marker of absolute authority, and that a dreadful fate looms for those who fail to comply.

Some are made to the specifications of the Inquisitor bearing them, while many others existed long before their bearer’s birth, created by those they may never meet. A Rosette could be an inheritance or gift from a predecessor, a holy relic used for millennia assigned to an Inquisitor in recognition of their pious deeds, or an artwork of its own right commemorating victories long since wiped from Imperial records. The diversity of Rosettes also lies deeper than in aesthetics, with some featuring internal data probes and many incorporating gene locks to ensure that only the Inquisitor and those they deem worthy can handle the rosette, where tamperers instead set off alarms or internal defence systems.

Inquisitors rarely allow their acolytes to use their unique Rosette. Instead, they often provide their acolytes with an emblem, pendant, ring, or badge representing their authority or, in rare cases, a sanctioned simulacra of their Rosette. Most operatives bear this symbol discreetly as part of their clothing or uniform, easily hidden or revealed at a moment’s notice — thereby bearing a sliver of their Inquisitor’s terrible authority into the field.

Not all Rosettes have a special function beyond representing the Inquisitor’s authority. However, you can use the following tables to roll for or choose a unique effect and form that fits an Inquisitor character’s or Patron’s Rosette.
