There is more to learn about each of the Holy Orders in @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.ZzHsqdssD6GJyhDE]{Patrons of the Inquisition}, and deeper lore still featured in the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.b06xyMjo4E4cYc40]{Roleplaying Inquisitors}.

Ordo Hereticus

Inquisitors of the Ordo Hereticus fight against corruptive elements hidden inside the Imperium — the @UUID[.YqpK5FPJW374jXHS#the-enemy-within]{Enemy Within}. Otherwise known as the Emperor’s Witch-hunters and most numerous in standing among the Holy Orders, it is their holy duty to capture or eradicate rogue psykers, mutants, and traitors, stamping out aberrant faiths before they run rampant.

Each Ordo Hereticus Inquisitor is just as sinister and feared as those they hunt. Their arrival on any world is met with much trepidation and awe as none know where their gaze may land and upon whom their suspicions might fall. Their eyes watch the Adeptus Terra fiercely, especially where those institutions have suffered corruption in the past.

An adroit Inquisitor will have informants everywhere, especially within these organisations, who may serve as future agents if they prove their loyalty. They also have close ties to the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.5Bx7K8k9VgjOZmA4]{Adeptus Ministorum} in fighting corruption and reinforcing aspects of the Imperial Creed. With the people’s eyes upon the Ecclesiarchy, the Inquisition recognises them as a powerful tool for spreading propaganda and encouraging the citizenry to surveil their neighbours.

Puritan Hereticus Inquisitors won’t tolerate any mention of heresy, watching their acolytes as closely as they would their enemies. Some might barely tolerate the existence of sanctioned psykers within the Imperium and may think of abhumans as another form of vile mutation. Radicals may well be more nuanced and see value in exploiting the heretics they hunt or their methods. They might allow a cult to continue operating (under careful surveillance) on the hunch that its activities lead to a greater evil operating in deeper cover. They think it is worth stabbing corruption in its heart, even at the expense of collateral damage.

Ordo Malleus

Inquisitors of the Ordo Malleus are the Imperium’s first line of defence against the @UUID[.YqpK5FPJW374jXHS#the-enemy-beyond]{Enemy Beyond} — unimaginable entities and daemons of the Warp, whose only purpose in our world is to corrupt, destroy, and feast on the souls of the damned. Known as the Emperor’s daemon hunters, the Ordo Malleus is tasked with purging daemonic activity, preferably before any full-on warp breaches occur. Time is always of the essence. Too late to stop such a catastrophe, they must face the resultant tide of horrors and escaped daemons at any cost.

The very existence of this Holy Order is a highly classified secret, even to other members of the Inquisition. To operate out in the open and better guard their secrets, Ordo Malleus Inquisitors often take on the guise of an Ordo Hereticus or Xenos Inquisitor. But when their time comes, these accomplished warriors, many of whom are powerful psykers, march to war clad in sanctified power armour, wielding ancient blessed weapons. Yet these Inquisitors and their acolytes stand alienated from the rest of Humanity; their knowledge and abilities are as much a strength as they are a lightning rod for the monsters they hunt.

Puritan Ordo Malleus Inquisitors strive to be incorruptible vessels of the God-Emperor’s righteous fury. However, those among the Puritans who do not recognise corruption as inevitable are bound to turn Radical without foreseeing their fall. Radicals among the Ordo Malleus recognise the potential of capturing daemons within hosts or weaponry to use their powers against their diabolical kin. They read forbidden tomes and consult with proscribed augurs, witches, or other sources to divine the means to vanquish their foe. They deem all this a necessary escalation of power against such an interminable foe; most discount the inevitable corruption that will swallow them up when the scales finally tip in their enemy’s favour.

Ordo Xenos

Inquisitors of the Ordo Xenos are charged to combat the @UUID[.YqpK5FPJW374jXHS#the-enemy-without]{Enemy Without }— the filthy xenos that attempt to invade, corrupt, and plunder the Holy Imperium of Man. Their ultimate ideal is to assert and safeguard Humanity’s total domination above all things alien.

Inquisitors of the Ordo often dedicate their lives and service to combating a single species above all else, for the number of different species in the galaxy is beyond count, and no one Inquisitor could efficiently fight them all. They may be called to a battlefront to lend their expertise in thwarting their studied enemy. However, they are more likely to operate around the edges of Imperium space, where the xenos threat is most diverse, and Humanity is more malleable to their corruptive influence.

The Ordo’s intent is to cut off any invasion before it even begins: seeking out and combatting secret infiltrations or campaigns of underhanded influence throughout the Imperium’s worlds. Many xenos species aim to gain a foothold by subverting weak-willed citizenry, tricking them with dazzling treasures and corruptive esoteric ideals. But make no mistake; these citizens are no less guilty than the xenos who corrupted them.

The most Puritan Ordo Xenos Inquisitors safeguard their Humanity without remit, declaring any xenos as unredeemable as a filthy daemon. They will purge first and investigate later, expecting the same of their acolytes. However, a Radical Ordo Xenos Inquisitor’s stance on Human superiority allows them to make tools of the xenos they encounter, deciding how to best exploit them before eradication. They may allow their acolytes to work alongside xenos mercenaries or wield xenos weaponry if necessary.

pages.name: Justice, Jurisdication & Investigation
pages.text:
‘I carry with me an Inquisitorial Seal. It is a small, unassuming object contained in a neat box. It is a modest thing. Relatively plain, adorned with a single motif and a simple motto. Yet with this little object, I can sign the death warrant of an entire world and consign a billion souls to oblivion.’

— Thraviam Flast, Ordo Malleus Inquisitor

Despite the average citizen’s belief that the Inquisition is effectively omnipotent, its Inquisitors cannot be everywhere at once — many crimes and injustices fall below what is worth their time and resources to investigate, and the same goes for their acolytes. Members of the Inquisition must consider their prime targets above all else, be it the daemon, heretic, or xenos. Sometimes, Inquisitors of the Ordo Malleus may be called upon to deal with a xenos threat. But, lesser infringements of any other kind are under the remit of the Imperium’s other factions and organisations and should be remedied by them.

It is rare that an investigation is ever a simple affair. Inquisitors and acolytes alike can dedicate years or decades of their lives towards pursuing a single threat or goal, with many of those years operating in total secrecy (see Long-Term Endeavours). Many investigations start subtly, with Inquisitor@UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.r6clx5uYnIpkdaRq.JournalEntryPage.56xpJ7ADckt2kxHB]{Inquisition Long-Term Endeavours}s aiming to thwart a threat before civilian awareness occurs. Inquisitors see their acolytes as small, precise, and expendable tools that can work in the shadows while overseeing their operations in a more public-facing form. Ultimate authority may be just that, but most Inquisitors know it works best when applied in the right place at the right time. Some investigations can pass a point of no return, where the Inquisitor is forced to rally troops and effectively march to war, with a greater potential for collateral damage and exposure.

Subtlety

@UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.KbejcPMug5gfoWWz]{Subtlety} encompasses a new ruleset to enhance Inquisition-focused campaigns. It grants rewards and sanctions for operating at different levels of covert behaviour. GMs and their Players should discuss implementing these rules before beginning or adding them to their campaign, ensuring that everyone understands the causality and benefits of their actions.

Inquisitorial Declarations

There are many official orders that Inquisitors alone can enact via their position. Some stand infamous for their impact upon the Imperium and the individuals involved. Acolytes should be aware of these declarations to the letter and knowledgeable of their dire consequences.

Excommunicate Traitoris: This declaration applies to those who have betrayed the Imperium through grand acts of heresy or any vile means that oppose the God-Emperor’s ideals. Any Imperium faction must eliminate or report the presence of any declared Excommunicate Traitoris individuals they come across, lest they tempt suffering the same fateful exile.

Exterminatus: The Inquisition’s infamous last resort. To unleash the ultimate sanction of Exterminatus upon a world is to consider it lost to damnation — an unavoidable scouring of all life upon a planet so that it is completely purged of corruption, often via excessive orbital bombardment or superweapon. Many citizens have heard legends, myths, or rumours of worlds that have been wiped off the star charts by inquisitorial order, but few know for sure. The Inquisition ensures that public knowledge of such events is expunged.

Extremis Diabolus: This declaration signifies an individual having cavorted with or been knowingly influenced by daemons. It often applies to rogue psykers or those practising forbidden arts; even some Inquisitors of the Ordo Malleus have been declared Extremis Diabolus after degenerating into Radical behaviour. It is similar to Excommunicate Traitoris but further acts as an extreme warning to stay away from such corrupted individuals.

Hereticus Absentia: This declaration is branded upon those, typically large groups, who refuse to comply with the Imperium’s laws and are often beyond the reach of Imperial authority. During the Macharian Crusade, many lost worlds were given an ultimatum to rejoin the Imperium or forever become its enemy — those who rebuffed the offer received this designation, forever to be treated no better than xenos.

ROSETTE Simulacra

It is rare for an Inquisitor to bestow their @UUID[.8VTOoxqcL2uC3eZm#the-inquisitorial-rosette]{Rosette} to any acolyte under them — but because they cannot be everywhere at once, some opt to provide their agents with sanctioned simulacra of their original. These copies may be further gene-locked to prevent misuse in the wrong hands or even have a timed window of use built-in before they become inert or self-destruct. Acolytes should be careful when bearing the Rosette publicly, as it may raise the stakes of their investigation in unforeseen ways or announce the Inquisition’s presence in places better served undiscovered.

pages.name: Desperate Measures & Escalation
pages.text:
When an Inquisitor’s mission spills into open warfare, or they encounter a threat no Inquisitorial warband could tackle, Inquisitors can call upon the aid of the Imperium’s military forces to respond in their stead. However, as with the scale of their 'limitless' authority, Inquisitors may need to make concessions regarding what forces they have access to and exert caution respecting potential consequences.

They may come to rely upon whatever forces are available nearby, stationed within their current or neighbouring systems. It may become a mission within itself to assert their authority. Calling upon any nearby large-scale force will significantly impact any world, upending local hierarchies and affecting the lives of most citizens in one way or another.

The most readily available forces are drawn from local lex enforcement, such as the Adeptus Arbites or Macharian Vigilites. Most worlds have garrisons of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-actors.Actor.ZIodTiyH9W5QBRU9]{Astra Militarum Troopers}, regiments of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-actors.Actor.bkP99HZ6JJ7IWd8U]{Tempestus Scions}, or an @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.HlxK2pbpx2Uio6bU]{Imperial Navy} presence in the system. These forces are the most commonly called upon and most likely to respond without expecting a trade-off — the Imperium working as it should. The @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.5Bx7K8k9VgjOZmA4]{Adeptus Ministorum} can raise a Frateris Militia to fight — a militia of devoted fighters whose lack of combat training is made up by their furious zeal. However, their loyalties might be complicated depending on where the Inquisitor’s target lies, measured against the local Ecclesiarchy’s interpretation of the Imperial Creed. Deploying these forces can close an iron grip of authority around the area, purge where necessary, and conduct specific missions where needed.

Inquisitors can call upon the Adepta Sororitas or the @UUID[.XJnH5b1jDXEtqkgF#space-marine-chapters]{Adeptus Astartes} to face more extreme threats. But these forces often have a will of their own; once they deploy, the Inquisitor and their acolytes are expected to stay out of their way. Each of these indomitable forces has its unwavering creeds and power structures to which they are bound. They believe they know best how to apply their power — so any unforeseen collateral damage may land on the Inquisitor’s head. The same could be said of the Officio Assassinorum, who can surgically remove challenging targets but operate within their own stringent rules for engagement where the Inquisition has little input. To be blunt, any forces called upon at this power level or beyond typically bring the acolyte’s involvement to a close, and they should move on to the next adventure.

The secretive Deathwatch and classified Grey Knights are any Inquisitor’s last resort against significant xenos or daemonic forces, respectively. Like their Space Marine brethren, these forces will enter the battle, execute their mission as they will, and leave just as rapidly as they deployed. Inquisitors are likely to expend significant resources cleaning up after their appearance, even purging innocent witnesses or razing what remains of the area of operations to cover their tracks.

This hierarchy of forces represents a vertical slice of the Imperium’s military might at large. But Inquisitors may have ties to other unique or scarce forces within the Imperium: those close to the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.nYfLVXh10BKR47Kj]{Adeptus Mechanicus} may have ties to call upon Skitarii warriors, those with ties to a Knight World may call upon the forces of an @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.B7MZBBT3bNew9N96.JournalEntryPage.X5EFP7IgIUx6CaBW#macharian-knight-houses]{Imperial Knight House}, or consider their ties to various @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.h6Z6Ia2q5RkRUlDG]{Rogue Traders}, and the forces under their influence.

Lasting Consequences

Many Boons listed in @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.ZzHsqdssD6GJyhDE]{Patrons of the Inquisition} allow an Inquisitor to call upon these powerful forces more readily through their close ties. However, players and GMs should be aware that calling upon these forces will likely cause a turning point in their campaign, often irrecoverably altering the landscape of their area of operations or shifting the balance of power far beyond their control.

Space Marine Chapters

Several Space Marine Chapters operate in and around the Macharian Sector, which often have ties dating back to the Macharian Crusade. The mysterious Minotaurs Chapter were dispatched during the Macharian Heresy to settle the ‘Euxcine Incident’, a conflict between the Doom Warriors and Interceptors Chapters whose remnants remain active in the sector. The Chapter fleet of the nomadic Verydian Hawks regularly pass through the Macharian Sector, coming and going from battlefields without any prior warning. Many Chapters have direct ties to the Inquisition and would aid an Inquisitor’s call, such as the Red Hunters — formed by the order of the Inquisitorial Representative on Terra, or the Exorcists — Space Marines experienced in combatting the forces of Chaos.

pages.name: Radical Methods
pages.text:
In their ongoing investigations, acolytes are constantly pushed further towards the edge of their understanding; many are forced to bear the burden of knowledge simply to survive or complete their mission. Sometimes, Inquisitors see the logic in fighting fire with fire, using the damnable knowledge of the Ruinous Powers against their own daemonic influences. Most Inquisitors hide these methods from others — for if they are revealed, they may find themselves condemned by their peers and branded as heretics in their own right.

This chapter discusses the use of Forbidden Knowledge as player character Skill Specialisations and the ramifications of characters receiving and displaying such knowledge. Later, we discuss the mechanics of possession and exorcism, tools often used by radical Ordo Malleus Inquisitors and their acolytes to bind or expel daemons from realspace.

pages.name: Forbidden Knowledge
pages.text:
The Imperium and Inquisition suppress information for an array of grim reasons. The most obvious reason for restricting information is that the education of vast swathes of Imperial citizens is not pertinent to the survival of Humanity. They only need to know how to perform their simple, drudging duty to the Emperor. This ignorance further serves two additional purposes: it protects the minds of those billions upon billions of souls, and it makes it more difficult for the heretic, the mutant, and the xenos to hide among them.

Ignorance is a shield for much of the Imperium. Knowledge of Chaos, the Warp, and daemonkind can make Human souls vulnerable to their sinister predations. Like a vile infection, the threat of Warp-dabbling practices and technologies could grow unchecked, making the impossible odds the Inquisition faces daily even more daunting. The weight of panic and terror that could grip the labouring population of the Imperium if they knew of the dangers of not just daemons but of heretic Astartes, traitor guardsmen, and insidious xenos surrounding the sector would be too much.

Indeed, burning zealotry and faithful ignorance protect many such citizens and make them anathema to Chaos. Many Inquisitors of the Ordo Hereticus believe ignorance is critical to preventing the spread of heretical ideas, and can often aid in their hunt and persecution of heretics. Infractionists and cultists can expose themselves by what they know, how they act, and how they respond to certain revelations. This is useful not just in observations but also in investigations and interrogations. Furthermore, when the Inquisition discovers an effective method of eradicating their foes, they ensure none know of their techniques so it cannot be foiled or turned against them.

Sources of forbidden knowledge often lie in the minds of heretics. They sprout their corruption when tempted to preach or eternalise their dangerous ideas and methodologies in writing.

Other times, forbidden knowledge results from unsanctioned encounters with xenos species; knowledge is rarely gifted but inferred through heretical curiosity. Some ideas are not damned until much later when denounced by the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.5Bx7K8k9VgjOZmA4]{Ministorum}, @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.3TtxuCzt0nNV1ysj]{Administratum}, or Inquisition. People who become heretics by this happenstance are sometimes purged to maintain order and purity but otherwise should learn quickly to forget what they know.

Examples of Forbidden Knowledge

  • A grimoire seized from a Chaos cult containing guidance on rituals to summon a daemon

  • Understanding aspects of the Warp pertaining to daemonic entities or psychic powers

  • A heretical text that analyses and denounces the God-Emperor as the saviour of Humankind

  • The knowledge to construct, operate, modify, or repair xenos or daemonic technology

  • Knowing the history or lore of any xenos species beyond what Imperial propaganda proscribes

  • Analysis or medicae reports related to the anatomy of a xenos species

  • Manuals or instruction in xenos or Imperium-restricted languages (such as Thoughtmark or Lingua Technis)

  • Any information otherwise redacted by Inquisitorial order

Gaining Forbidden Knowledge

The Talent @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.Lbm6mRMiqSGHq9GD]{Forbidden Knowledge} is a requirement for a character to gain various proscribed Skill Specialisations, including Linguistics (Forbidden), Lore (Forbidden), and Medicae (Forbidden). A character cannot purchase the Talent without the permission of the GM, but there are some situations wherein the Talent might be granted to a character to represent the mechanical consequences of a narrative development.

Example

In the course of an Inquisitorial investigation, Acolyte Despina comes into possession of a terrible tome looted from a Chaos-worshipping heretic. She decides to study the tome to learn more about the heretic, their cult, or what power they might be serving so that she may more effectively eradicate the Emperor’s enemies. The GM decides that such a study would require a Difficult (−10) Linguistics (Cypher) Test to decipher the grotesque scrawl and a Difficult (−10) Discipline (Composure) Test to resist the corrupting influences of the tome. Despina succeeds in both Tests, and the GM determines that she gleans a few clues as to the cult’s beliefs and other activities and access to the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.Lbm6mRMiqSGHq9GD]{Forbidden Knowledge} Talent.

While some Inquisitor Patrons are willing to impart dangerous knowledge upon their acolytes, knowing it could be helpful for the battles ahead despite the dangers of such knowledge, others are unwilling or untrusting. Inquisitors vary significantly in their philosophical approaches to their unending duty to the Imperium. Some seek plausible deniability in their acolytes by telling them little, whether they have a Radical or Puritan approach. Other Patrons tell their acolytes lies, like the greater Imperium; this might be for protection, or, depending on the nature of the Patron, it might even be a test. It is essential to consider how the Inquisitor treats their acolytes concerning knowledge, how they approach forbidden knowledge, and how it might affect other connected individuals. For example, is there a rival Inquisitor waiting for an opportunity to condemn them, or do they have Contacts among other Factions that also endeavour to learn forbidden knowledge?

Using Forbidden Knowledge

Forbidden knowledge can serve as a remarkable temptation for Radical Inquisitors and acolytes. Many Inquisitors would use a daemon’s true name to banish them; why are the steps toward more esoteric understandings of daemons and the Warp so immediately terrible? Knowledge is power, and the Inquisition fights on dangerous fronts of knowledge and the unknown, struggling to rationalise and make sense of what they encounter.

Depending on the source, forbidden knowledge is simply that: knowledge. This could involve information about the enemy's nature, strengths and weaknesses, and how to fight or banish them effectively. This could include discovering the true name of a daemon and the means to banish them. It could also include learning more about a specific xenos species, such as the weapons they use and how to detect, track, and fight them. Knowing this information could grant the characters @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf.JournalEntryPage.3j1kargHBeCTssE7]{Superiority}, which can help turn the tables in their favour.

The Imperium and Inquisition play a dangerous game with knowledge, especially forbidden knowledge. By censoring knowledge about Chaos, the Warp, daemons, and various xenos topics, the individuals who express knowledge of these topics expose themselves to the Inquisition and other interested parties. This can play an essential part in investigation; if an NPC knows too much about a given topic that the Imperium considers forbidden or censored, the characters should be able to notice that and act on it.

The Burdens of Knowledge

Learning and possessing this knowledge is fraught with peril, not merely from the dangers posed by other elements of the Inquisition or faithful members of the Imperium. Regardless of its form, some knowledge is so dangerous that it might exact a physical and spiritual toll or is so desired by various factions that the character is never safe with it in their possession. Some manifestations of forbidden knowledge are corrosive, corrupting, and subversive. They might be forbidden tomes of Warp knowledge that twist a character’s perspectives of reality. Other information might be highly desired for the advantage it could give over other factions, xenos species, or the cosmos itself.

Example

At the end of a raid on a cultist hideout, Icharus discovers a peculiar item on the leader’s remains, something they were desperately reaching for during the fight. It is a cube of dark, iridescent metal, marked with symbols that writhe and crawl. The cube whispers with a hissing, sibilant voice. Icharus wants to give it a cursory examination to determine the item’s nature, so the GM has him make a Difficult (−10) Lore (Forbidden) Test. Putting the clues together and succeeding on the Test, Icharus learns the cube is covered in forbidden sigils, and within it, a daemon is contained, able to answer questions and bequeath knowledge. Later in their investigations, Icharus uses the box to learn something about their ongoing investigation. The GM asks him to make a Difficult (−10) Extended Test that requires 6 SL, requiring at least one Lore (Forbidden) or Linguistics (Cypher) Test to make sense of the cryptic whispers and one Fortitude (Endurance) Test to resist the corrupting effects of the black cube. Each Test takes an hour, and each failed Test inflicts 1 point of Corruption. Possession of such an item could attract unwanted attention, especially from those who can identify the daemonic nature of the cube. It could result in Chaos cultists seeking to retrieve it and even members of the Ordo Malleus seeking to execute the acolyte and destroy the box.

Example

A team of acolytes are investigating a strange area of a feral world that is believed to be the source of psychic disruptions affecting the locals. After parsing ancient legends and rumours and crewing an expedition to ancient sites, the team find a curious structure jutting from the environment. Kappa, the tech-focused Savant, investigates the structure with a Tech (Engineering) Test. With an incredible roll, Kappa learns that the structure forms an Aeldari Webway gate. While Kappa spends time learning more about the structure, rumours of the Webway gate escape their expedition. This draws the attention of an Ordo Xenos Inquisitor, who prepares to hunt them down. Furthermore, Kappa’s Contact within the Adeptus Mechanicus reaches out to get the information from him. Thanks to his investigation, should any xenos emerge from the Webway gate, the acolytes will be prepared and gain Superiority for avoiding surprises and fighting from prepared positions.

Example

In their persecution of a rogue psyker, Drusilla and her fellow acolytes discover a tome among the renegade’s possessions. Drusilla spends some time examining the tome, and determines that it is an instructional tome on manipulating the power of the Immaterium, useful for psykers who might seek to expand their repertoire beyond what the Imperium sanctions. In secret, Drusilla seeks to learn from it new powers she might leverage against their foes. The GM asks her to make a Difficult (−10) Extended Test that requires 6 SL, requiring at least one Linguistics (High Gothic) and Psychic Mastery Test to follow the techniques presented and at least one Discipline (Psychic) Test to resist the energies of the Warp drawn to the unsanctioned and unfamiliar techniques. Drusilla succeeds in learning a new Psychic Power, knowing that more remain within the tome, but there is a strain upon her mind and soul.

When the secret is out

If other entities in the world discover the characters are hoarding or learning from forbidden knowledge, many narrative consequences might arise. These could include garnering attention from other Inquisitorial agents or even the interests of heretical agents, like cultists or Infractionists.

The Inquisition and its collected philosophies and approaches are divided. The Puritans of the Inquisition believe that possession of this knowledge is the first step on the road to the Radical and then the heretical. They think that by accepting this lore, this knowledge, the Inquisitor and their acolytes become damned and may end up serving the enemy. Other, more Radical approaches believe that only by knowing the tools of the enemy can true victory be achieved. Radicals often turn the tools of the enemy on themselves, wielding dangerous weapons, and consorting with xenos and daemonhosts to better ensure the Imperium stands another day.

For example, hunting a daemon or intending to bind it to a vessel for imprisonment often requires knowledge of the Warp and daemonkind, which is not common even among the Inquisition. Those who walk the Radical path claim that it is worth the danger of corruption to uncover tools that prevent and banish daemons or even turn those daemons against Chaos itself. Some Radical Inquisitors believe to know the Great Game of daemonkind, enough to turn the murderous forces of Khorne against the hedonites of Slaanesh, or the sorcerous changers of Tzeentch against the foetid daemons of Nurgle. Others believe this is the path of pure heresy and nothing more.

Severity of Forbidden Knowledge

Ordo Hereticus

Ordo Malleus

Ordo Xenos

Minor

Contact with Infractionist characters known to work with Radical Ordo Hereticus agents — such as hereteks, rogue psykers, and smugglers

Identifying knowledge of daemons, Chaos, and cults that would otherwise be censored

Knowledge of xenos wargear, how to obtain it, and how to use it

Major

Knowledge of Warp sorcery and forbidden psychic powers outside the bounds of the Imperium

Knowledge of how to summon and bind daemons, such as using daemonhosts or making Daemonblades

Knowledge of xenos services, and how to contact and use them, such as xenos bounty hunters or guides through frontier space

Consequences of Forbidden knowledge
Societal Response

  • Possession of forbidden knowledge attracts the attention of Imperial authorities (Arbites, Ministorum investigators and ultimately other Inquisitors) who seek to eradicate that knowledge and cleanse any in the Imperium — including the characters — who have learned of it.

  • The characters attract attention from among their enemies, who seek to claim the knowledge they have, or further tempt them away from the Imperium — such as daemons willing to bargain, or perfidious Aeldari who seek to manipulate the characters in their xenos schemes.

Negative Results

  • Cult knowledge, the tools of infractionists, and consorting with abhumans or the wretched can weaken faith in the Imperium, and stain a soul akin to gaining Corruption.

  • Knowledge of using recidivist resources could spread, impacting Subtlety.

  • Interaction with tomes of Chaos, knowledge of the Warp, and more conveys Corruption.

  • Any resulting daemonic activity in the area could cause Psychic Phenomena, thereby impacting Subtlety.

  • Interaction with xenos creatures or wargear/devices can break the mind, or leave a stain on the psyche, equivalent to Corruption.

  • Knowledge of consorting with xenos entities could spread, impacting Subtlety.

Positive Results

  • Identifying cults and their differences. Gain Superiority when fighting related enemies.

  • Knowledge of how to banish daemons and their capabilities. Gain Superiority when fighting related enemies.

  • Knowledge of their tactics, weapons, and capabilities grants characters Superiority when fighting related enemies.

pages.name: Possession & Exorcism
pages.text:
Among the enemies of the Imperium, even amidst the enemies of Chaos itself, there are few who are so corrupting and so malicious as the daemon. One of the greatest dangers such entities pose is their ability to possess a living soul, walking realspace in their shoes, with the potential to wreak unchecked havoc. While psykers are typically the most vulnerable, any creature — excluding those with the Pariah Gene — could face the danger of possession. The daemon could hide within its vessel for a time before any of the signs of possession manifest, allowing it to scheme and plot. And a possessed psyker, empowered by the madness and power of a daemon could unleash cataclysmic misery upon whole worlds.

The dangers of possession can arise in a campaign that faces Chaos, and the threats of daemons and the Immaterium. This might involve investigating and eliminating a Chaos-worshipping cult who seek to summon a daemon, offering one of their members as a host, or they might be tracking an individual already possessed, leaving a trail of destruction and corruption in their wake. The danger of daemonic possession could even be levelled against NPCs, such as those who fight alongside the characters or serve as Contacts and informants. Worse still, the characters themselves could face the danger of possession.

Defining Daemonhost

Daemons and daemonhosts are Chaos incarnate. Much information surrounding daemons and how they function is vague and sometimes contradictory. Daemonhost is a term used for a mortal whose body has been prepared to host a daemon’s will or has been used in the past. However, the specifics of possessing a physical body vary greatly. As a GM, you can play into this, or determine how it works for your campaign in a way that better serves your narrative.

Transparency And Consent

Daemonic possession is not something to be trifled with — it is a horrendous fate from which most never recover, a loss of agency and identity every bit as substantial as death itself. As a GM, you should be careful before allowing a player character to fall victim to possession. It robs them of their agency, and, if handled authentically, will ultimately alter the player character's personality, goals, values, and more. Survivors of daemonic possession are rare, their insights into the nature of daemons are often valuable, but only if their psyche has survived the experience.

As a GM, you should not inflict this fate upon a character unless you are certain their player is an enthusiastic participant in the dark storytelling that must, by necessity, follow. This can be done simply by asking them, either at the table or between games. During play, be sure to telegraph what is happening and give them plenty of opportunity to plausibly escape. Make it clear, for example, that they are entering the lair of an unnatural entity, or that a cult they risk capturing has designs on binding a daemon into mortal flesh. As with most storytelling, foreshadowing a threat will make it more impactful, and will avoid springing a threat on players without the opportunity to prepare for it. Inform players that they can burn @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf.JournalEntryPage.8UpBUTEErWslyTdW]{Fate} to avoid possession (permanently reduce their fate to overcome a dire circumstance), giving them the opportunity to veto the experience should they wish.

If you think a player character becoming possessed may be a significant feature of your game, it is best to talk to your players about it well in advance. The best time to do this is session zero, as presented in @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.f5PuitUGgp6jQz5K.JournalEntryPage.I3c3gLHRa8Fv3kV9#session-zero]{Imperium Maledictum}, and should certainly be discussed if your players are considering working for an @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.brh2O5CexxurRbM7.JournalEntryPage.YFKg8L1rfWbScqkr#ordo-malleus]{Ordo Malleus} Patron.

As always, remember the golden rule — Imperium Maledictum is a game and should be enjoyed by all its participants. If something would make a player, as opposed to their character, uncomfortable, just don’t do it.

The Effects of Possession

Daemonic possession varies greatly, united only by the severe danger it poses. Over time, or rather quickly in the case of a sudden and forceful possession, the vessel will become twisted by the unnatural energies of the Warp, twisting into a horrible abomination. Daemonic possession has a limited duration. Eventually, the vessel will be consumed and destroyed, causing the daemon to return to the Warp, becoming exorcised. A possessing daemon has wildly different goals from another, they might simply seek wanton destruction or a more complex and subtle plan of corruption. Only the extremely fortunate individual can survive the harrowing process of possession and then undergo the rigours of exorcism, removing the daemon, and leaving the vessel alive.

Characters who face possession will not typically face a dramatic and total possession. Instead, it will normally be the result of failing to deal with the consequences of exposing oneself to various things; forbidden tomes, forbidden knowledge, bargaining for secrets, or exposure to psychic powers and perils of the Warp. When the narrative opportunity arises, it should be clear to the players the consequences of engagement and failure. The controlling player and the GM should work together to understand how the daemon affects the character, and how this affects roleplaying. Determine how the daemon might prey upon specific emotions or motivations of the player, and how the daemon might twist these for its own goals. This is also true of NPC possession, as a GM consider how the presence of the daemon can affect an NPC’s personality over time. The GM should consider the type of possessing daemon. Sometimes this will be a natural effect of the narrative; if the characters are specifically hunting a daemonic nemesis, you should have a strong idea who this daemon is, what it wants, and what it is capable of.

Example

Icharus, the acolyte who recovered a daemonic black cube from a raid on cultists, has used the cube to learn more about their enemies, and has gleaned forbidden knowledge from the daemon trapped within. Throughout their investigations, Icharus has earned Corruption from the cube, and in his latest attempt to learn something from the cube, he miserably fails his Discipline Test. The GM knows that the daemon wants out of the cube, and Icharus has suffered Corruption from its use.

A bridge has been made, and with the player previously well-informed about the consequences, the GM decides that the box fails to answer, and Icharus gains Corruption. Worse still, though Icharus will not know immediately, the daemon has begun to possess him. The GM can use the bestiary to find the profile of a daemon that matches; a @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-actors.Actor.CAvzgSBWrbnHu8zi]{Pink Horror}, a daemon of Tzeentch, matches the kind of daemon that would be bound to such an item.

Characters possessed by daemons ignore the upper cap limits of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf.JournalEntryPage.PuzopCeKzYgcYAwh]{Corruption}, ignoring when they have more Mutations than their Toughness Bonus or Malignancies more than their Willpower Bonus. Under daemonic possession, their Corruption levels can skyrocket, relating to how deeply the daemon has dug their claws into the character’s soul.

As a possessed character gains Corruption, they progress along the Possession Tracker. When they are first possessed, the character gains 2d10 Corruption immediately — which can cause them to gain Mutations or Malignancies as normal. When a character gains enough Corruption to reach the threshold of another possession type, they change.

Possession Tracker

Corruption Levels

Possession Type

Resisting/Controlling the Daemon

01-30The PuppetDifficult (-10)
31-60The GatewayHard (-20)
61-99The VesselVery Hard (-30)
100The ChosenImpossible

The Puppet (01-30 Corruption)

A subtle form of possession, the daemon remains within the Warp but uses a conduit or channel to the victim to begin to suffuse their soul with part of its daemonic essence. The puppet is usually unaware of what is occurring, but the daemon can begin to exhibit control over the puppet’s actions, behaviours, and even their perceptions.

At this stage, the daemon can attempt to exert minor control over the possessed character by encouraging and empowering certain behaviours. When the possessed character attempts a Skill Test that matches the Skills of the possessing daemon, the GM can have the daemon add +2 SL to the Test, but the character gains 2 Corruption. The possessed character can attempt to resist with a Challenging (+0) Discipline (Composure) Test, decreasing Corruption gained by 1 point for every positive SL.

The Gateway (31-60 Corruption)

The victim becomes aware of the possessing daemon — perhaps as it progresses from a prior possession — and the daemon begins to exert more influence over the victim, temporarily taking full control in violent or chaotic blackout moments.

During moments of heightened emotion, when the character is at risk of gaining Corruption, or when the GM decides it serves the narrative, the daemon can attempt to exert control over the character. The controlling character can attempt to resist by making a Discipline (Composure) Test, the Difficulty determined by the Possession Tracker Table. If they fail, the daemon takes control for a number of minutes of narrative time, or 1d5 rounds plus 1 additional round for every −1 SL. Additionally, the character suffers 1 Corruption for every −1 SL on a failed Test.

Unleash the Daemon

A possessed character can draw upon the daemonic energies within them to gain leverage during a battle or gain an edge when making a Test. The controlling character makes a Discipline (Composure) Test, the Difficulty determined by the Possession Tracker Table. If they succeed, they can choose to gain one of the following bonuses:

  • +2 SL to a Skill Test that matches the possessing daemons type, such as Awareness or Lore for Tzeentchian Daemons; Rapport or Reflexes for Slaaneshi Daemons; Fortitude or Medicae for Nurgle Daemons; and Athletics for Khornate Daemons.

  • Gain the use of a Talent associated with the daemon, or at the GM’s discretion, for a number of hours equal to the character’s WilB + the decimal number of their current Corruption.

  • The character gains a surge of vitality and recovers Wounds equal to their WilB + the decimal number of their current Corruption.

The controlling character then gains 1d5 Corruption. If the character fails their Test, they still gain the boon for a single Action or a single minute of narrative time, but the daemon then takes control as if the character had failed to resist the daemon.

The Vessel (61-99 Corruption)

In the case of sudden possession, or as the result of the daemon gaining more control, the victim’s mind and soul are imprisoned and put to one side, and the daemon wears their flesh without restraint. It is only a matter of time before the rampant mutations and corruption become untenable for the flesh. There are very brief windows wherein the victim can, for mere minutes, gain some control over their body once more.

Possessed characters can fight for control of their body and attempt to wrest it away from the daemon for a very short period of time. The character can do this a number of times per day equal to their Willpower Bonus (WilB). They make a Fortitude (Endurance) Test, Difficulty equal to resisting the daemon in the Possession Tracker Table. If they are successful, they assume control for 1d5 rounds plus 1 additional round for every +1 SL on the Test, or if using narrative time, the same number of minutes.

The Chosen (100+ Corruption)

Those devoted to Chaos may open themselves up to a daemon, freely allowing it to possess their body and wreak havoc, or an unfortunate character may have had one trapped inside them for a considerable amount of time, scraping away at its confines, aiming to take total control. The character is possessed as normal, but the daemon gains full control immediately.

Whenever the chosen daemonhost is required to make a Test or take an Action, they can assume the characteristics of the vessel or the daemon, gaining 2 Corruption each time they use the daemons characteristics. Furthermore, the daemon can Unleash the Daemon anytime it chooses, gaining Corruption and warping their flesh vessel without restraint.

A character who gains 100 Corruption while possessed will gain this possession type. There is no hope for a character when they reach this point. The daemon within can choose at any time to wholly sacrifice the vessel to manifest in realspace.

The @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-actors.Actor.M6XWkYc0lfuKl2hU]{Daemonhost} represents a character in The Vessel stages (61–99 Corruption). They begin with 70 Corruption, or otherwise choose a number within this range when deploying them.

Exorcising Daemon

Mortals who become possessed by a daemon rapidly succumb to the suffusing Warp energies, the rampant and unceasing corrosive stain upon their souls, and the madness that seeps into the mind twists their perceptions and taints their thoughts. Senior members of the Inquisition and @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.HURMpEU0Nnc93Ocv]{Adeptus Ministorum} argue about the potential for exorcism, what methods work, when and why to attempt it, and whether it is even possible. Many would insist that once possessed, it is better to destroy both the vessel and the daemon and be done with it, while some more Radical Inquisitors see the potential use in a mind and soul touched by the Warp and the powers of a daemon.

An exorcism can be attempted for a possessed individual. It is believed an exorcism, rooted in the occult and forbidden, can take many forms. Preparations, and methods, vary greatly. Some are approached as a test of faith, surrounded by icons of the Emperor, specially crafted incense choking the air, and clerics singing and chanting hymns and prayers. A more profane approach might involve symbols of banishment, occult and forbidden phrases and words of power, and the sacrifice of pure and corrupt souls in exchange for the vessel. Daemons are so multitudinous in form and will that no singular method works against all.

The potential for exorcism is a decision left to the GM. It might involve an Extended Test at a Difficulty determined by the current Corruption, as seen in the Possession Tracker Table. The Extended Test could use Lore (Forbidden), Psychic Mastery (Various), and Discipline (Composure) or Discipline (Psychic), though the GM may reward creativity or careful and thematic preparation. The SL of the Extended Test is determined by the Corruption total of the possessed individual. When the SL reaches the Corruption total, the daemon is exorcised, and the character regains total control over their body once more. They immediately gain the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-items.Item.YacxYO0U5ssj2aee]{Tainted Vessel} Talent at no cost.

Summoning Daemons

Cultists, in their accursed rituals, often attempt to use a daemonhost to summon daemons into realspace. As the GM, you can handle this in a purely narrative sense or reverse the method of exorcism previously described to track how far along their summoning ritual they are, corrupting the vessel over several rounds or days given their timescale. Consider the cult making an appropriate Test and adding their SL to the vessel’s Corruption, eventually reaching 100 Corruption or beyond to manifest the daemon.

Binding Daemons

Characters can attempt to bind daemons, taking their essence from the Warp and containing it within a physical medium — be it a damned Daemonhost, holy relic, or technological construct thought to be strong enough to include it. Characters may wish to pursue this dangerous method to seal a threat away for an extended period, capture the daemon in question to extract fell knowledge from it, or exploit the monster for its raw power.

Conducting the ritual requires the characters involved to make a Group Extended Test similar to the one described in @UUID[.yMUESh1wlAuqgNSp#exorcising-daemon]{Exorcising Daemons}, except here they should aim for a certain number of successes, determined by the daemon’s Role:

  • Troop = 25 Successes (Minor Exposure)

  • Elite = 50 Successes (Moderate Exposure)

  • Leader = 75 Successes (Major Exposure)

Additionally, characters can pursue the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.r6clx5uYnIpkdaRq.JournalEntryPage.56xpJ7ADckt2kxHB#learn-a-true-name]{Learn a True Name} and @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.r6clx5uYnIpkdaRq.JournalEntryPage.56xpJ7ADckt2kxHB#prepare-a-ritual-of-binding]{Prepare a Ritual of Binding} Long-term Endeavours in advance to prepare and strengthen themselves for a binding, gaining the benefits described in each Endeavour.

GMs are encouraged to generate complications throughout this ritual: have the daemon lash out at the characters, attempt to possess one of them, try to distract them, or affect the surroundings. Characters involved must make a Test to resist the levels of Corruption listed on this page. Substantial failures or Fumbles throughout the ritual could increase the Difficulty of their Extended Test or easily result in an effect generated from the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-tables.RollTable.9aSbu2mswOOI43J1]{Psychic Phenomena} or @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-tables.RollTable.2YYlAUyaVIt4bZVa]{Perils of the Warp} Tables.

@UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.r6clx5uYnIpkdaRq.JournalEntryPage.56xpJ7ADckt2kxHB#prepare-a-ritual-of-binding]{Binding a daemonhost} this way results in the host starting with Corruption equal to the successes on the corresponding Extended Test thresholds listed on this page. Physical contact with relics used to bind a daemon becomes a source of Corruption, the amount depending on the Role of the daemon trapped within.

pages.name: Running Inquisition Adventures
pages.text:
Every Imperial institution exudes fear as a measure of control and authority, some more underhanded than others. The @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.HlxK2pbpx2Uio6bU]{Imperial Fleet}, @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.6Yav4onpokz5e5jg]{Astra Militarum}, and Adeptus Astartes wield the fear of raw military might. The @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.cvpsLwcsXf4myIpK]{Adeptus Administratum} brandishes regulations, procedures, and weaponised bureaucracy to oppress those outside their inner circles. The @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.HURMpEU0Nnc93Ocv]{Adeptus Ministorum} and @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.nYfLVXh10BKR47Kj]{Adeptus Mechcanicus} preach fears of countless unknowns and depravities, offering a lonely beacon of purity or righteousness as succour. In their grim ways, the Imperium itself is a bastion built upon terror.

Yet all of them pale compared to the visceral fear exuded by the Inquisition — its agents are everywhere and nowhere, all-seeing and all-knowing, implacably ruthless and utterly remorseless. It is this pervasive, insidious construct of lurking dread that you, the GM, have the pleasure and challenge of bringing to life in all its dark and sinister glory.

In running an Inquisition-focused adventure, a GM is freed from many of the usual constraints wrought by the other institutions of the Imperium. While other organisations hold a stiff bureaucratic chain of command with policies and procedures to go with it, these are quickly subordinated to the immediate needs of Inquisitors.

There are simply too many threats across too much space which must be dealt with immediately — and if bureaucracy must be set aside to do so, so be it. Inquisitors have almost unlimited authority for good reason: they are fighting an unending war to save Humanity’s soul.

Inquisitors and their acolytes are essentially free to go anywhere, to compel testimony from anyone, to bring any person under scrutiny for potentially consorting with dangerous xenos or vile forces of Chaos. This gives you far more freedom to develop adventures that will take the characters into places they would not usually get to go: the heart of an Adeptus Militarum bastion or an Imperial Fleet voidship, the innermost sanctum of an Ecclesiarchy cathedrum, the fume-filled depths of an Adeptus Mechanicus forge world, or the gleaming spires housing the nobility atop a hive.

Moreover, since the role of Inquisitors is to find and destroy the lurking threats chewing at the inner stability of the Imperium, you are free to confront the characters with nearly any manner of enemy, from a vicious Drukhari raid erupting from a Webway portal to a sanity-blasting incursion of vile daemons from the Warp. Inquisition adventures allow you and the players to explore the Imperium from its most glistening heights to its foulest depths — and confront the myriad wonders and terrors they will find there.

pages.name: Inquisition Maledictum
pages.text:
By its nature, the Inquisition is a profoundly secretive institution. Though perceived to operate under a hierarchy and by sets of policies or rules, the Inquisition does so loosely. It is, in fact, more of a ‘purpose’ than an organisation. It is an eclectic collection of disparate individuals and their retinues, all generally acting towards what, in theory, is a common goal — seeking and eliminating overt and covert threats to the Imperium.

Just how Inquisitors operate is very much up to the individual. Some are dour figures of menace, while others are effusively charming. Some are scrupulously honest and believe in conforming rigidly to the codified laws of the Imperium. In contrast, others believe the means are irrelevant as long as their ends are achieved. Some are pure and noble, righteously sending thousands to their deaths to preserve the sanctity of the Emperor’s realm. Others are corrupt and desperate, selling their very souls to embrace the unhallowed powers of their enemies, telling themselves they are only doing so to strike down the nightmares that plague them and the Imperium.

Inquisition games in Imperium Maledictum can span various themes and atmospheric settings. And since Inquisitors are empowered to go anywhere and compel testimony from anyone, they can be set in nearly any part of the Imperium, from the murky depths of a hive’s sump to the decayed glory of a planetary governor’s palace. That said, there are common threads that will wind through all Inquisition games.

Foremost among these is an investigative focus. While Inquisitors often confront obvious and overt threats, they most commonly hunt things that do not wish to be found. A surreptitious incursion of Drukhari seeks to harvest souls and feast on their suffering unseen. A blasphemous cult insists on sinister secrecy until their fiendish ends are achieved. Inquisition games, therefore, tend to focus on finding clues and using them to piece together a picture of who the enemy is and what they are doing — often a difficult task in itself due to the widespread repression of information in the Imperium (see @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.uzQAAUFfkNu8TZOi.JournalEntryPage.75evxRXWoYG9mizR]{Forbidden Knowledge}).

Subtlety

The advice presented in this chapter goes hand-inhand with using the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.KbejcPMug5gfoWWz]{Subtlety} Mechanic . Further details and advice for implementing this mechanic are presented in @UUID[.tuASnDHy4WyxFVOZ#subtlety]{Running Investigations}.

Only when a threat is fully identified will an Inquisitor mobilise the resources needed to stop whatever malfeasance is underway. However, not all Inquisitors have equal access to the resources they are ostensibly pledged, and many demand that their investigating acolytes put their souls even further at risk to combat their unspeakable foes. Investigation-focused games require forethought and planning. It is essential that the clues the characters uncover are relevant and will lead them towards a greater truth. Even red herring clues must fit logically into the story, but they should not distract the players for too long or too far from the truth.

Because Inquisitors tend to work in the shadows, paranoia is another theme common to Inquisition games. Until an enemy is identified, they could be anyone. And even then, they could have agents and allies willing to act on their behalf nearly anywhere, at varying levels of culpability. Threats are often layered, where solving one mystery merely reveals another beneath it. Deception and obfuscation wielded like weapons can throw the Inquisitor off the trail. Even those considered trustworthy can be suspect — bribery, blackmail, and extortion can turn even the most reliable ally, and differences in philosophy occasionally lead to Inquisitors hunting one another. At its heart, the Inquisitor's unspoken creed is quite simple: trust no one.

The result is a game that often shifts through shades of grey. While some things — heretical cults, xenos conspiracies and the like — are starkly harmful and wrong, many others will be more nuanced. A planetary governor withholding tithes to ensure their people do not starve violates Imperial law, but a starving world may soon produce no tithe. The best Inquisition games force the players to confront difficult choices and often choose between the lesser of numerous evils. That said, you should not deny your players the periodic satisfaction of finally confronting and overcoming a clear and present threat. Endlessly ambiguous games will, eventually just become frustrating!

How to make it feel like Warhammer

The Warhammer 40,000 universe is a unique and diverse gothic-inspired science fiction setting. Beyond the intricate histories and characterisations, new players and even GMs can often forget aspects of what makes this setting what it is. The following points represent constants in the world, all interlinked, that permeates everything in the setting. Take them to heart when crafting stories and running game sessions, and pass on the themes and tones to your players.

Physical Scale

Everything is massive all the time. Humanity has grown into a population of quadrillions spread across a million worlds, most of whom live in thousand-layer hive cities. Even when it comes to structures and utilities, most buildings, even the doorways and windows built within, seem needlessly massive. People travel between the stars on cathedral-like voidships larger than any skyscraper. Press upon your players how small they are in the grand scheme.

Timescale

In the Imperium, things rarely happen in an instant. Characters might spend years mired in an investigation, travelling between planets or systems, or stuck in the glacial tide of the Administratum’s bureaucracy. As GM, your ability to skip ahead in time is vital, but do not forget to press upon your players the time spent — you can punctuate this by filling up their years with extended downtime activities (see @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.r6clx5uYnIpkdaRq.JournalEntryPage.56xpJ7ADckt2kxHB]{Inquisition Long-term Endeavours} in the Inquisition Player’s Guide).

The Imperial Creed

Its unique history and religious grasp affect everyone in the setting, whether they adhere to it, reject it, or are rejected by it. Most citizens have grown up in lifestyles where they visit temples and grand cathedrums every week to pay respects to the God-Emperor of Mankind and receive sermons to bolster their piety. Yet the scale at which the Imperial Creed reaches and the divisions of the void in between leave room for dangerous interpretation by both zealots and quiet detractors.

Conflict

Like the Imperial Creed, the God-Emperor’s war machine touches every soul in the Imperium in one way or another. Every citizen knows someone who has been shipped off to fight on some far-flung war-torn planet. Entire forge worlds and their populations are devoted to manufacturing arms to feed the front lines. This eternal war can never stop; if it did, the status quo would crumble, and Humanity would fall to its innumerable enemies.

Fear

On some level, everyone is terrified. Forces within and without the Imperium press the dire need for compliance and duty to every citizen; where faith falters, fear must take its place. Everyone has someone breathing down their neck. This fear starts at the top of the Adeptus Terra. It trickles down through the controlling factions of the Adeptus Terra and the ruling nobilities to the labouring citizens at the bottom. No citizen has any natural choice in the matter — who in their right mind would trade their everyday plight for the uncountable and unknowable enemies clawing at the Imperium’s borders?

Technology

Despite the fears and restrictions imposed upon technology in the Imperium’s laws and strictures, it is rare for a character to be without some kind of technology on their person or as part of their daily lives. Humanity is reliant upon technology to survive. Machines to recycle breathable air, generate food, fight for survival, or replace a lost limb. Yet despite advances, not everyone has access to everything they need. Technological inequality is so vast and staunchly defended that aspects known and studied by some are myth and magic to others.

How to make it feel like Imperium Maledictum

Imperium Maledictum operates within a unique area in the Warhammer 40,000 setting — one close to the ground among the citizenry of the Imperium, dealing with the plights that fall upon them from forces internal and external to their lives. It often centres around Machiavellian patrons caught between the demands of duty and ambitions for power who use people as pawns to further their goals. The following points represent what playing Imperium Maledictum should evoke in your players and what makes it a unique experience. Keep these points in mind when running games and building your own stories.

Noir Themes

Stories in Imperium Maledictum are often set in the dirt, far from the Imperium’s frontlines. Characters have a dark and nihilistic outlook on life, doing their best just to get by. Prominent themes in the setting are corruption, criminality, and inequality, which in this setting can manifest as heresy or even the heavy hand of purity. Nothing is ever black or white; the narrative hinges on moral quandaries and ambiguity, choosing the lesser of malefic evils.

Gothic Themes

The world’s atmosphere leans on gloom and decay, coupled with constant oppression, unknowns, or impending threats. Most characters have some kind of tragic backstory, even if it is just their station in the Imperium — yet they are forced to be barbaric, superstitious, or unenlightened. Turning points come from supernatural events that are often challenging to explain and accept — horror and suspense surround these mysteries, and it is up to the players to explore them.

Deadly Encounters

It is easy for player characters to be harmed and just as likely to die, especially when diving into combat unprepared. As GM, using the threat of violence is often more important than enacting it. Perpetuate this threat throughout the world — the Imperium is an unforgiving and violent place, no matter where you look — and it will keep the tensions high and create many more dramatic moments for your players to enjoy.

Brains and Brawns

Characters should be able to solve situations as they best see fit. Violence should not be the go-to answer. Characters can pick apart their problems intelligently. Investigate, politick, and make dubious alliances and deals. Sometimes a challenge can even be overcome by filing the correct paperwork. The GM’s job is to facilitate the wealth of options available to their players and drive home the consequences of their actions.

Patrons and Agents

The player characters have a unique partnership with their Patron and an unequal one at that. What does the Patron want from them, and what can they get in return? The Patron may provide them with rare comfort and safety but is often within their power to ask for unreasonable sacrifices in return. The GM’s job is to perpetuate the Patron’s involvement in the narrative — they should constantly pressure the player characters and be an unignorable part of their lives, for better or worse.

Find Leverage

Players should be challenged to leverage every advantage they can find. Players need to think critically. Investigate their surroundings and the factions and alliances they have access to, and scrape together what they can. The GM should place obstacles in their way, evoke the labyrinthine nature of the Imperium, and remind them that nothing is ever free. This aspect can manifest mechanically through the game’s Influence and Superiority systems and new contacts and clues that appear along the way.

pages.name: Setting Up Your Game
pages.text:
Just as an Inquisitor and their agents must arm and prepare themselves for a mission, so must a GM prepare to run an Inquisition game in Imperium Maledictum. Some GMs may be quite capable of crafting a nuanced, layered, investigation-focused game ‘on the fly’, but for most, it is a good idea to ensure as much as possible is in place before the first die hits the table.

Crafting the Story

The first step is determining the ‘core concept’ — a one-sentence description of the story. For instance, ‘The characters will investigate a Drukhari incursion in the sump of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.B7MZBBT3bNew9N96.JournalEntryPage.59y8WFXTbwKRwiRI]{Hive Voll}, only to find that the xenos are in league with an ambitious minor noble of @UUID[Compendium.impmal-starter-set.journals.JournalEntry.Vjfxkwi1rFYPnSIf.JournalEntryPage.Dml6BI69jLrNOQU0#castyx]{House Castyx}’. From this, you can derive a story’s essential three acts: the beginning, middle, and end.

  • Beginning: The characters are given their mission by their Patron to investigate rumours of a Drukhari incursion in Voll, after which they encounter the sinister xenos.

  • Middle: Complications ensue as the characters uncover evidence that the Drukhari are in league with a member of House Castyx while continuing their efforts to deal with the xenos.

  • End: Having uncovered sufficient evidence to implicate the noble, the characters receive assistance from their Patron through a squad of Deathwatch to finally destroy the xenos, then confront the noble with their crimes.

For each of these ‘acts’, you can derive story beats — the important scenes or events within. For example, in the first act, the beats may include ‘the characters meet with their Patron and are given their mission’, followed by ‘the characters travel to Voll, enter the lower hive and examine the scene of the first Drukhari incursion,’ followed by ‘the characters have their first, brief skirmish with the Drukhari’, and so on. You can then plan for each beat to be a scene, encounter or other event and can prepare settings, NPCs, loot and the like for each.

Each beat should flow logically from the one to the next. @UUID[.tuASnDHy4WyxFVOZ#clues]{Clues} are a key way to advance the story within beats, but they can also link beats together. Some beats and the clues given in them can also be decision points, where the characters will choose to send the story in one of several possible directions.

For example, if the characters have discovered a xenos weapon that requires analysis, they may consider taking it to the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.9frbPZ9v3lFR9Kva]{Adeptus Mechanicus}. But if they have another clue suggesting that the Adeptus Mechanicus may be involved in the corresponding xenos plot, do they find another way to analyse the weapon, which may take more time and at a greater expense?

You may only wish to develop a detailed story up to a decision point and then allow the players to decide where they want to go at the end of a session. That will allow you to continue developing the story following that choice and save you time from developing detailed story branches that may never be used! The number of such beats can vary. Fewer beats will result in a quicker, less involved story that is easier to set up, while more beats will provide a longer, more detailed story that also involves more work to create and run. It is up to you and your players to determine which works best for them based on their available time, and interests.

You should consider what resources you need for each story beat. NPCs, for instance, can be drawn from @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.2TukBjlkS5RG5Qka]{Contacts}, @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.SJPyRkdBEOCtmD8R]{Sector Threats}, or the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ]{Bestiary}. However, if you require specific NPCs, such as unique villains, you will have to adapt one already existing or even create one from scratch. You may want to prepare ‘read aloud’ text so you can flavorfully present all of the information players need to be immersed in a scene and do it in a way that captures the mood they desire, be it creeping dread, visceral horror, bureaucratic tedium, or something else.

Memorable NPCS

NPCs should be distinctive and memorable. To assist with this, you can portray them with a particular voice and speech mannerisms suitable to their Faction and describe their appearance and dress in unique ways. The tables in @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.uJURMn2glWHhjqJk]{Imperium Maledictum} can assist with this. NPCs should also serve a purpose in the story. Being antagonists or allies is an obvious aspect, but tricky NPCs can also possess (and perhaps try to conceal) clues or other information that would be useful to the characters' investigation.

Preparing the Game

With your story in hand, whether a premade module or one of your own devising, you can now prepare for your next session. The following suggestions intend to assist a GM in doing just that.

Patron Review: Review the Patron’s Boons, Liabilities, and Motivations. Also, review the Goals, Philosophies, and Techniques of the Patron’s Ordo and their particular Philosophy. Finally, review their Influence with Factions that will be, or are likely to be encountered by the characters during the story. Knowing these things will help you roleplay the Patron during the game. Creating a Patron whose words and actions are consistent and whose expectations of the characters are clear will greatly increase the game’s immersion while helping the players roleplay their characters.

Character Review: Know the characters! A common pitfall for GMs is to focus on knowing their ‘side’ of the story but not that of the characters. In particular, you should consider how to advance not just the story of their game but also that of the individual characters. If a player has decided that their character has a sworn enemy, for instance, then inserting clues regarding that enemy’s actions and whereabouts will move that story forward and further invest that player in the game.

Skill Review: Determine which Skills and Specialisations are likely applicable to your story beats, when specific instances of Advantage or Disadvantage might apply, and when particular Tests would be Opposed, Extended, or even revealed in Passive Tests. Drawing on each player character’s skills can give them each their time in the spotlight. However, it is unnecessary — nor even possible — to be exhaustive, as the players will likely do things you did not anticipate. Nonetheless, presetting particular Tests will make it easier to keep things balanced and save time.

Strengths & Weaknesses: You should also know the characters' strengths and weaknesses, what they can do well and what they cannot. This will assist you in setting up Tests that will be within the characters' abilities. If a particular clue or other piece of information is essential to move the story forward, then knowing the characters' stats will assist in setting up Passive Tests that will still allow players agency and their moment to shine. This avoids the risk of awkwardly stalling the game as a result of a failed Test.

Rules Review: Likewise, consider which rules are likely to apply to the game in general and the upcoming session, and ensure you are conversant with them. Suppose you expect the session to see the characters buying, selling, and trading for new equipment. In that case, they should review @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.wqlquQ8Njtd5fb4Y]{Armoury} of Imperium Maledictum, particularly the section on @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.wqlquQ8Njtd5fb4Y.JournalEntryPage.k5sND1C17nY9xB1G]{Trading Equipment}. Likewise, suppose you expect a session with a great deal of combat. In that case, they should ensure they have good knowledge of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf]{Rules} of Imperium Maledictum, and particularly the sections on @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf.JournalEntryPage.5wEY1d4xaZf5cEiq]{Combat}, @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf.JournalEntryPage.UaRHLqZ99zmg7AeE]{Damage, and Wounds}.

Notes Review: Finally, you should review any notes they made at the end of the previous session. It is worthwhile to invest a few moments at the end of a session in making notes, capturing any points that would be relevant at the outset of the next session. This includes details like changes in character Influence with various groups, any Temporary Influence in effect, and the characters' Superiority Level. By being prepared — knowing the characters and their Patron well, having a well-crafted story ready and knowing the relevant rules and mechanics — you can minimise friction and wasted time at the table and provide the players with a smooth, immersive, and exciting game.

Let the players lead

Against the alien and the traitor, there is no fair way to fight.

The players will routinely face the deadliest of foes and impossible situations. Try to lean into their ideas! Superiority will often tip the scales, turning disaster into a pyrrhic victory, so entertain their wild ideas. The Inquisition is one of the few Imperial Factions to embrace pragmatism, no matter how slight. When preparing for your next session, consider what your characters are capable of and how they might use their most favoured Skills and Talents to solve the problems that arise.

Planning your campaign

A campaign in Imperium Maledictum is effectively a series of interconnected missions but with enough wiggle room to compensate for players making either interesting or terrible decisions. Building an Inquisition focused campaign typically begins with choosing one significant idea to focus on and then building missions to weave in and around this idea as characters progress towards a final confrontation. You must decide what this big idea is. Thankfully, the Inquisition is embroiled in so much activity in the Macharian Sector that you have plentiful options to choose from. Consider some of the following ideas to serve as a starting point or simply inspiration:

  • The characters' Ordo Hereticus Patron is working to eradicate false scriptures of the Imperial Creed. They have heard whispers of a cult tearing down Lord Macharius’s reputation and history. This cult plans to build power and assault Macharia to undermine the Imperium’s control in the sector.

  • The characters' Ordo Xenos Patron has heard whispers of Genestealer Cult activity working in the underbelly of a hive city. Tackling the cult, they discover links to other Genestealer Cults on other worlds and the involvement of a Polypsykana Inquisitor, who has been manipulating the cult to study their psychic abilities.

  • The characters' Ordo Malleus Patron has discovered a Horusian Inquisitor is secretly operating in the sector. Their acolyte cells must be rooted out, the daemons they hunt destroyed, and the Inquisitor themself brought to justice.

  • The characters' @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.brh2O5CexxurRbM7.JournalEntryPage.0vHms9BJQGOVa0dO]{Thorian} Patron is scouring the sector for Aeldari artefacts, hoping to reverseengineer their technology to aid the God-Emperor’s return to realspace. They are being hunted on two fronts: by the Aeldari, whom they are tricking and stealing technology from, and by their Puritan peers, who see their interest in xenotech as heretical.

  • The characters' @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.brh2O5CexxurRbM7.JournalEntryPage.R7LueEsDUhrSYHNn]{Amalathian} Patron is investigating the fall of several noble houses in the sector, discovering a series of Drukhari assassinations — unbeknownst to them, they are secretly at war with a @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.brh2O5CexxurRbM7.JournalEntryPage.7Aqg1D2wSmKjmzWj]{Recongregator} Inquisitor, in league with the xenos, who seeks to tear down ruling houses they believe are false claimants to their authority

  • The characters' @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.brh2O5CexxurRbM7.JournalEntryPage.UAWh0hEvWDwob6CT]{Isstvanian} Patron is working towards promoting war against xenos factions in the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.B7MZBBT3bNew9N96.JournalEntryPage.UbH7oOtTYfjFlKRt]{Gallosque Nebula} but has garnered the unfortunate attention of an @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.brh2O5CexxurRbM7.JournalEntryPage.R7LueEsDUhrSYHNn]{Amalathian} Inquisitor who does not wish to risk the status quo.
