A shadow war has broken out between the two Inquisitors. Can the characters' Patron simultaneously defeat their rival Inquisitor quietly whilst stoking the flames of war in the Nebula?

Besides incorporating the characters' Patron, some of the best campaign ideas hinge on the Inquisition’s @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.brh2O5CexxurRbM7.JournalEntryPage.DvP1i46KYTgkMN0W]{Philosophies} and the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.SJPyRkdBEOCtmD8R]{Threats} the Imperium faces; it is even better if your campaign can draw on both.

The Patron’s chosen Philosophy can be the core of your campaign, a concept to thread throughout each mission — the outcome of a mission should help them further their goals, safeguard their tenets, or put their ideals into question. At the end of your campaign, you may see the Patron achieve their goals or see them utterly dashed. This outcome should be up to the actions of your players' characters and what they achieve. Do they wish to see their Patron succeed? Do they think their Patron has gone off the deep end into Radicalism and is no better than the enemies they have been fighting thus far? How do these outcomes play into their survival?

The Macharian Sector has traditional Threats aplenty: heretics, xenos, and daemons, but do not forget to include aspects of the Adeptus Terra, noble houses, Infractionist elements, or even opposing Inquisitors and their retinues within that category. Narratives are often more interesting when the lines are blurred between everyone involved. Introducing another Inquisitor to the mix halfway through the campaign can be a great ally or enemy, depending on how they relate to the Patron’s Philosophy or goals (see @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.b06xyMjo4E4cYc40.JournalEntryPage.FLhAj7NDZUgL1Nls#between-inquisitors]{Between Inquisitors}).

Test run

Before embarking on a full-blown campaign, it might be worth creating and running a few individual missions with your playgroup. This gives you, the GM, and your players time to understand their Patron and characters. Furthermore, it is an excellent source of inspiration for gauging what aspects of the Inquisition your players are most interested in and, oppositely, what they dislike.

Structure

Beyond the core concept, your campaign is built up as a series of missions, as described in @UUID[.zsrszpZRzjT4fDWf#crafting-the-story]{Crafting the Story}, considering that elements from one mission feed into the following or future aspects of the campaign overall. Similar to the three-act structure presented in Crafting the Story, a similar approach can be applied here, with each act containing a handful of missions. A short campaign could have as many as one or two missions per stage, scaling up as appropriate and increasing the stakes for all involved as the campaign progresses.

  • Early Missions: Here the stakes are planetary-level. Send the characters on a few missions, let them get a feel for investigations and explore roleplaying their characters. As this act closes, you must establish the characters' ultimate enemy and their Patron’s driving goals and Philosophies. Use these first few missions to reveal these aspects piece by piece.

  • Middle Missions: Up the stakes, the whole system or subsector is at risk. Have the characters spread out their investigations, hop from planet to planet chasing down leads, uncover related heresies, and confront lower-level aspects of their enemy’s organisation. But all of this is to reveal more of the more significant threat they are yet to face.

  • Final Missions: Up the stakes one last time; now the threat could affect the whole Macharian Sector or harm a widespread aspect of Imperial culture and society. By now, the characters will have done most of their investigating against their prime threat and acquired some scars. In this closing act, line up the characters' enemies and have the characters tackle each one head-on.

Remember to give your players downtime between each mission (see Between Missions, in both @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.eUFS6mIQy2oiz6IX]{Imperium Maledictum,} and the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.r6clx5uYnIpkdaRq]{Inquisition Player’s Guide}), and grant them regular contact with their Patron through @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.b06xyMjo4E4cYc40.JournalEntryPage.1diRtTeN2hbZUhOY]{briefing and debriefing} sessions. Remember to hand out rewards as you go, as indicated in @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.f5PuitUGgp6jQz5K.JournalEntryPage.qsaLi310r4uyLu4R#rewarding-players]{Rewarding Players}.

Consider adding a @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.FNEW8e33IisZh27W.JournalEntryPage.Y1wjtyi7JdgHxQiF]{Conclave to these between-mission segments}, or it can be a mission in and of itself. Have the characters and their Patron encountered such a sector-spanning foe that they should involve the Macharian Inquisition? Have they garnered enough evidence of heresy against a Radial Inquisitor to petition for a declaration of Excommunicate Traitoris from their peers?

Railroading

It is essential to plan out the major arcs and pillars of your campaign, but listen to your players on a mission-to-mission basis. Build each subsequent mission, considering the ideas and avenues they wish to explore based on the @UUID[.tuASnDHy4WyxFVOZ#clues]{clues} you gave them. An exceptionally rigid series of events and missions can lead to railroading — forcing your players and their characters into something they do not want to do or explicitly laying the track out in front of them — which you should always strive to avoid.

Remember: Your job as GM is to facilitate the stories your players create due to the stage you set up for them to play on and generate consequences for their actions, both for their characters, the setting, and the cast of NPCs involved.

However, creating such an open sandbox sometimes leads players and their characters to get lost or pursue clues that are deliberate red herrings. The key to getting them back on track is rarely to tell them what they did was wrong — instead, it is to reward them for the avenues they have pursued and then show them what the campaign’s prime antagonist has been doing in their absence. You can use this tactic as a GM if your players feel like they need a break from the larger narrative or if you need time for your antagonists to achieve something in the background.

You can use similar tactics when branching your narrative, giving players a choice of multiple missions to pursue or clues leading to different avenues of investigation or locations. But time is always of the essence. If they pursue one mission while ignoring the other, what happens due to their choices or neglect? Does it mean they gain something from succeeding in one mission, whereas their enemy gains ground elsewhere? There should be a balance, or the choices you put before them will feel unfair. Any narratives that branch outwards should come back around — they find more clues or information that lead back towards the primary threat or narrative.

pages.name: Running Investigations
pages.text:
Given the investigation-heavy nature of many Inquisition games in Imperium Maledictum, a GM must consider specific aspects of their story. Giving thought to these in advance will help you run an immersive and seamless game that is not plagued by unintentionally misleading clues, inadvertent investigative dead-ends, or having the story derailed by the unexpected use of a character’s Equipment or Psychic Powers.

Daemon's in the details

A fine mind is a blessing of the Emperor; it should not be cluttered with trivialities.

Do not worry about tracking every minute detail! Your players will remember the dramatic narrative and tense moments more than they will remember precise mechanics. Use the game's mechanics, like Subtlety and Influence, to guide the game’s narrative. And if something creates friction for your game or your players, remove it.

Clues

Clues are pieces of information or physical objects that players discover during play, allowing them to advance the story. They may present as weapons, a bloodstain, an article of clothing, or even statements made by NPCs or entries in a personal journal. Regardless, clues should rarely remain hidden from the characters; their true meaning should be obscured. All clues must fulfil two conditions to be useful — they must be relevant to the story, and coherent.

Being relevant is self-explanatory. An irrelevant clue will not help advance the story and may simply stall it. This does not mean a clue’s relevance must be immediately apparent. For instance, the importance of a bloody footprint in a corridor may only become evident when the characters discover a gruesome murder nearby. This is not to discount clues intended to be deliberate red herrings, but even these must be designed so their misleading nature eventually becomes clear. An oily footprint, for example, has no immediately apparent relationship to a murder. It is ambiguous and may waste game time unless you remove the ambiguity and demonstrate its relevance by having the players discover a clear link between it and the murder.

This is not to say that clues cannot be deliberately misleading. Such red herrings can certainly heighten tension in a game, but they should be used sparingly. Moreover, the players should be able to determine their misleading nature quickly. To do otherwise risks frustrating the players, needlessly slowing the game down and lessening their engagement.

Where you place a clue also matters, as is how it is presented. In general, rarely hide a clue from the players, especially one that begins a thread to more definitive ones. What is more critical is obscuring the meaning behind the clue — do not hide a bloodstain, but obscure the meaning of it. Give the players something to chew on. Oddities like this should stand out against the background of the scene, or revealed on a relatively easy or opportune search.

A clue is coherent if it flows logically from what came before it and points the players to what comes after it. For instance, a bloody footprint could point the players towards the footwear of various suspect NPCs. This could lead the players to examine that footwear, finding another clue: a boot with a distinctly matching print. That could then, in turn, lead the players towards a suspect or even to another clue — perhaps information indicating that the boot’s owner has not worn that pair in months. Suggesting that the suspect is being set up could open a whole new line of investigation for the players.

As an aid to developing good clues, you can consider working backwards. For instance, if you know where you want the players to get at the end of a particular beat, you can design clues in that beat and the preceding ones to lead them there. And do not forget the three things commonly taken to prove a suspect guilty of a crime — means, motive and opportunity. Designing clues that will assist in revealing those aspects (and clues that point at those clues) will ensure that clues are relevant and coherent.

Note that some clues may require forensic or deeper analysis. If the characters do not have the means, this is an opportunity to engage other Factions related to the investigation or locale. For instance, an NPC from the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.cvpsLwcsXf4myIpK]{Adeptus Administratum} may be able to verify the authenticity of some paperwork — if the characters have or can gain the Influence to arrange it. Furthermore, offering the characters more than one clue at a time is often interesting, creating branching paths in the investigation. A selection of clues can be solved at different times, always giving the players a thread to follow if they believe they have come to a dead end.

Tests

Tests are described in detail in @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf.JournalEntryPage.EwKNNdQ5EYayCPdA]{Rules}. Make sure you are familiar with those rules before you continue!

Tests may be required if the characters undertake actions during their investigation that transcend what would reasonably be basic knowledge and understanding. For instance, simply finding a bloodstain on a bulkhead does not require a Test, but discerning the significance of its spatter pattern does. You must balance using Tests against the need to keep the story moving and the players engaged. Too many Tests are time-consuming, and too few renders the players choice of Skills and Talents irrelevant.

You must also decide what to do about failure. If the PCs can fail a Test to identify the meaning or message of a cryptic sigil scrawled on a bulkhead, that information should never be so critical to advancing the plot that it brings your story to an absolute halt. In that case, what is your ‘fallback’? To continue this example:

  • The PCs could find someone (an NPC or Contact) to analyse the sigil definitively (thereby taking more time or incurring a debt).

  • The PCs could search for more instances of the cryptic sigil (or similar) in the area, leading them to other potentially connected locations (thereby taking more time or forcing them to explore dangerous parts of the world).

  • Alternatively, the PCs could uncover another clue in the vicinity that points in a similar direction (thereby delaying the revelation of the sigil’s meaning until later but letting them continue their investigation).

Similar consideration should be given to the degree of success expressed by the Test’s Success Level (SL). For instance, if the characters achieve an Astounding Success in the Test to identify the sigil, is there additional information that you could impart to them about it? They could discern the sigil’s meaning at the base level of success. But with greater success, they could identify the cult that wrote the sigil and, even more so, learn what Chaotic deity they align themselves with.

For this reason — dealing with failure or unanticipated success — you should, as much as possible, plan the Tests that the PCs will have to conduct during their investigation. Especially take into consideration the concept of ‘failing foward’. There is nothing worse for the players' investigation and investment in the story than a dead end. How can your players continue their investigations, analyse clues and track down suspects when they fail a critical Test? The answer should allow them to continue pursuing their threads but with more obstacles — they should still be able to succeed, but must work at it to do so.

For example, when setting up a bloodstain clue, you could determine that a Test to identify the species will use the Medicae Skill with the Human Specialisation and that the PC performing it will gain Advantage if they have the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.gzG57HKU32iQBSkO]{Pathologist} Talent or use a @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.kous2Ot3MNPfthuo]{Diagnostor}. Having set the parameters for the Test, if PCs fail, they will still be able to obtain a sample that can be reliably analysed by an unhelpful NPC chirurgeon, costing them some time. An Impressive or Astounding Success in the Test will reveal not just the species but other traits related to the individual. By establishing this beforehand, you will be ready to deal with the Test and its outcome when it comes up in play.

Passive Tests

As an alternative to Tests, you can employ ‘Passive’ Tests. These forego the normal procedure for making a Test entirely. Instead, you can determine that some clues can simply be provided to a player if they have particular Skills, Talents, or Equipment. This provides a distinction between a PC with no relevant experience or training in a subject and one who does have it, without requiring a Test.

For example, say your characters are examining the scene of a battle between Gangers and Cultists in the lower levels of Hive Rokarth, trying to discern how events played out. If one of the characters has the Awareness, Intuition, or Logic Skill or the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.C4qz5xdqvEPUt9Un]{Combat Master} Talent, then instead of making a Test, you may simply rule the character can reasonably reconstruct the events of the battle without a regular Test.

The advantage of such ‘Passive Tests’ is that it can reliably provide the players with information that will help advance the story. This is useful for story-critical information, meaning you do not have to worry about the consequences of a failed Test. It still allows that player or character to shine, showcasing their hard-won skills and knowledge.

Using a Passive Test does not preclude a subsequent regular Test. The combat-savvy character in the above example may be able to unravel the progression of the battle, but they may have to make a regular Test to identify the specific weapons involved.

Downtime Ponderings

@UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.r6clx5uYnIpkdaRq.JournalEntryPage.z9PTik4AMrYlbVhR#litanies-of-recollection]{Litanies of Recollection} is a group or individual Endeavour that characters may undertake between missions. The party, or the character, may use discussion, meditation, and reflection to consider what they have learned so far in the course of an investigation.

This may allow them to realise that they have missed important clues, see connections between clues that may not have been obvious, or otherwise ‘remember’ information that will assist in moving their investigation — and the story — forward. You could also consider allowing the characters to spend Fate during a session to realise that they missed something

The sort of Test this may involve, or whether it involves a Test at all, is up to you. In the absence of a Test, you may simply wish to give the players an important clue they missed, reasoning that their extended period of quiet, contemplative reflection and discussion caused them to realise it.

A Passive Test, as described above, is another way of giving the players the information they are missing. This is a good way of dealing with missed or misunderstood clues, with the trade-off being that the characters are not able to undertake other Endeavours while engaged in the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.r6clx5uYnIpkdaRq.JournalEntryPage.z9PTik4AMrYlbVhR#litanies-of-recollection]{Litanies of Recollection}.

Alternatively, you may wish to use the opportunity provided by the Litanies of Recollection to provide the players with new insights and revelations based on the information they already have. This is a good time to use an @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf.JournalEntryPage.EwKNNdQ5EYayCPdA#extended-test]{Extended Test}. Successes accrued during each attempt provide a small piece of useful information, with a major revelation if the characters succeed overall. These successes could result in the characters having Advantage in subsequent Tests related to clues when they resume their investigation.

Technology

Technology can greatly aid in the conduct of an investigation. The usefulness of some types of technology is obvious — for instance, an @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.dO7XoDXD9QYTy6zZ]{Auspex} would be helpful in locating a hidden recording device by detecting its emissions, while an @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.paXqMCUFqcpVEEBE]{Excruciator Kit} could help compel testimony from an unwilling prisoner.

However, you should remain open to innovative uses of technology possessed by the characters. For instance, a character may propose using a @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.Yp1Fmiml09wxHj4h]{vox bead} as a temporary impromptu bug to listen in on a meeting between leaders of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.GPqYZykonC12TJb1.JournalEntryPage.5jO3tXI5hSEBAC4s]{Infractionist} gangs, a @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.qjjlckQ3WvF4KLxO]{Chirurgeon's Kit} to assist in determining if a dead body has been surgically altered, or a @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.kous2Ot3MNPfthuo]{Diagnostor} to help to identify blood and tissue samples. While such uses might technically fall outside a strict reading of these items as described in Imperium Maledictum (particularly the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.wqlquQ8Njtd5fb4Y.JournalEntryPage.A1aeWZR8mZ0Kd98e#tools]{Tools} section), they likely do fall within a reasonable envelope of capability for them. However, such unusual uses may require difficult Tech Tests, and may even be seen as blasphemy by some purists from, for instance, the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.9frbPZ9v3lFR9Kva]{Adeptus Mechanicus}.

The investigative nature of Inquisition games also means that some sorts of often overlooked technology may be extremely useful. For instance, assume the characters diligently use a @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.rgkUmSGkBrOKvo5p]{Pict Recorder} and a @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.h1g1g9Rrjt7CnYeW]{Dataslate} to record their ongoing investigations. You may wish to give Advantage on some subsequent Tests, grant Superiority, or even offer some benefit to @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.r6clx5uYnIpkdaRq.JournalEntryPage.z9PTik4AMrYlbVhR#litanies-of-recollection]{Litanies of Recollection}, any action that would benefit from having detailed and objective information collected earlier.

The @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.AMVwCpsT9ISRY65Z]{Emperor's Tarot} (and any similar sort of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.RJQOgOg4q8krADXi]{instrument of divination}) is another useful way of imparting important information to the players, but it should be a more indirect sort of insight, given its mystical and prophetic nature. For instance, the Emperor’s Tarot may not point directly at an incriminating document secreted in the files of an @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.cvpsLwcsXf4myIpK]{Adeptus Administratum} NPC known to the characters. It may, however, offer a glimpse of endless rows of stacked documents being ceaselessly sorted by dour, blank-faced figures. Such a portent should be enough to get the characters at least considering their Contacts in the Adeptus Administratum for a closer look!

Psychic Powers

Psychic powers are detailed in @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.3mzwixuzgerGUpu1]{Imperium Maledictum}

The Inquisition has a complicated relationship with psychic powers. On the one hand, psykers represent a profound, even existential threat of the very sort that the Inquisition — and particularly the Ordo Hereticus — seeks to expunge from the Imperium, or at least strictly contain them by aiding the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.upGG1JZPDbC7dpJJ]{Adeptus Astra Telepathica}. On the other hand, psykers can be a powerful addition to an Inquisitor’s retinue, both to wield psychic might offensively and to defend against the psychic powers of their enemies. Assuming that one of the characters or an NPC cooperating with them is a psyker, the question of using psychic powers to further an investigation will inevitably arise.

Setting aside the myriad and complex issues around the legitimate use of psychic powers and their ramifications, such powers can be helpful as an investigative tool. You should allow the characters to employ their powers as they see fit — again, of course, being mindful of the potential consequences of using them, but of potentially being seen to be using them. Again, setting those matters aside, how much information should the characters be able to derive from psychic investigation?

Some powers have obvious applications to investigation. For example, @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.Qc4Adi2niwAoeY1j]{Preternatural Senses}, @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.UxhvWWKjI4rkQFii]{Psychic Scrutiny} and @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.plATcbLJsFW1evOT]{Soulsight} can all assist in gaining information about and locating clues at a crime scene, while @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.XuFiBvRR2vT9IPeC]{Spectral Hands} may assist in retrieving clues from otherwise inaccessible locations. @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.sZluux2xrMuK4w1H]{Mental Interrogation} can pry critical information from a suspect. Various powers of Divination, such as @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.xfNouLz2vwT0L7Gr]{Question the Warp} and @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.3vquTkVELDNBVsZL]{Psychometry}, can help the characters unravel what may have happened and the motivations of those involved.

The players themselves, though, may come up with innovative uses for Psychic Powers to assist them. For example, a character may use @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.nsW4ViB2r0oIfyKp]{Dull Pain} or @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-items.Item.tNcKq3ZaMDeogkh3]{Seal Wounds} to ease the injuries of a wounded enemy in an attempt to make them more willing to reveal information — this could take the form of @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf.JournalEntryPage.qxkAEAcB9xAl56Xa#temporary-influence]{Temporary Influence}. You should remain open to such novel uses of Psychic Powers.

Generally, you should view the characters’ use of Psychic Powers as another useful way of providing them with information and clues. To that end, when creating a story, you should try to anticipate when the characters are likely to attempt to use Psychic Powers and prepare accordingly. And, if the characters begin to rely on them too much, the rules for Psychic Powers offer built-in limiters, such as accumulating @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.3mzwixuzgerGUpu1.JournalEntryPage.buydA5mPJln97Qk5]{Warp Charges}, manifesting @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-tables.RollTable.9aSbu2mswOOI43J1]{Psychic Phenomena}, and triggering @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-tables.RollTable.2YYlAUyaVIt4bZVa]{Perils of the Warp}. Even if these things do not themselves result in disasters, they can attract unwanted attention to the characters and make their investigations more difficult!

Expert Assistance

There are several ways that the players may engage with expert assistance during the course of a game. The most obvious is taking advantage of their @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.2TukBjlkS5RG5Qka]{Contacts}, either by making use of their Patron’s Influence with that Contact’s Faction, or their own @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf.JournalEntryPage.qxkAEAcB9xAl56Xa#personal-influence]{Personal Influence}, potentially boosted by @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf.JournalEntryPage.qxkAEAcB9xAl56Xa#temporary-influence]{Temporary Influence} in the form of bribes or blackmail. Clever players may make note of potentially incriminating evidence of wrongdoing uncovered during the course of an investigation, but instead of simply bringing the miscreant to justice, they may hold onto that sinister knowledge to use as Temporary Influence later.

If the players do so, you should consider the sort of information that these Contacts might reveal. Even if the characters have considerable Influence with a Faction, members of that Faction are unlikely to undermine their own interests. For instance, if an officer of the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.6Yav4onpokz5e5jg]{Astra Militarum} is involved in a profitable conspiracy to skim tithes from an Imperial world, then that officer is unlikely to assist the characters in uncovering that same conspiracy, no matter how much Influence they bring to bear — unless, of course, they can otherwise convince that officer it would be worth their while!

Not all expert assistance will necessarily come from using Influence with Faction Contacts, however. You may decide to simply make expert assistance available, if it would help advance the story. For example, in order to provide the characters with forensic expertise they do not have, you could simply stipulate that their Patron’s retinue includes an NPC retainer with that expertise. This could allow the characters to focus on finding the clues, such as the evidence itself, that will advance their investigation — the exciting part — rather than spending time and effort finding some way to analyse the samples — a likely less-exciting prospect.

Superiority

@UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf.JournalEntryPage.3j1kargHBeCTssE7]{Superiority} is a resource which can fundamentally reshape a battle or encounter. It can be used to increase the SL on a single Test during a turn of combat, and is also compared with NPC @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.dZFX8HOdsFDpI7l0#resolve]{Resolve} to determine if those NPCs become @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.hdElQAwiBr5AyoRf.JournalEntryPage.3j1kargHBeCTssE7#resolve]{Desperate}.

Of the three ways given in Imperium Maledictum to gain Superiority, the results of an Inquisitorial investigation most obviously apply to two — Know Thy Foe and Know Thy Battlefield. In the case of Know Thy Foe, clues uncovered during the investigation may reveal critical weaknesses that can be exploited. For example, assume the characters find evidence of nothing but strikes by melee weapons at the scene of a suspected massacre perpetrated by a Drukhari raiding party. They may be able to infer from this that the Drukhari in question either do not have, or preferentially do not use ranged weapons in combat. If the players specifically draw that conclusion, then you should consider giving them +1 Superiority with respect to those Drukhari.

Similarly, suppose the characters discover a blood trail they believe to be left by an injured cultist fleeing into a safehouse somewhere in the lower levels of @UUID[Compendium.impmal-starter-set.journals.JournalEntry.Vjfxkwi1rFYPnSIf]{Hive Rokarth}. In that case, they may be able to discern a likely destination. They could then use this information to learn more about the location from residents of the lower hive or @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-actors.Actor.gQxTENJSdTQTVfDM]{Vigilites} who have patrolled the area. Again, if the players make this connection, it would be reasonable to give them +1 Superiority for undertaking such forward-thinking preparations.

Note, however, that you should only grant Superiority if the characters draw a suitable conclusion from the results of their investigation. In the second example above, if the characters find the blood trail but do nothing but simply follow it, then a Superiority bonus would not be justified. It is not sufficient to merely find clues to gain Superiority — the players must take the next step, using those clues as the basis for inferences that would warrant a Superiority award.

When you are preparing your story and designing your clues, it is a good idea to make notes of what sorts of conclusions drawn from them that would prompt you to give a Superiority award. This is not to suggest this would be exhaustive — the players may come up with other conclusions that are just as worthy and you should remain open to them. However, it is another way of saving time during play, while also making it less likely that you will miss an opportunity for the players to earn Superiority.

Subtlety

The Inquisition Player’s Guide introduces the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.KbejcPMug5gfoWWz]{Subtlety} mechanic to Imperium Maledictum. This optional ruleset provides a framework for GMs and players to dynamically adjust the world and characters in response to how covertly or overtly the players approach objectives. On the surface, it is an excellent tool for players to judge how well their characters and decisions perform and gain a small reward. But on a deeper level, it will enable you, the GM, to do the same.

The rules contained in the Inquisition Player’s Guide outline the mechanics for players and GMs alike; consider the following advice:

  • When using Subtlety, you secretly track the party’s actual rating. The party has to spend time in or around their mission to figure out (and not always successfully) what their Subtlety rating is every time they want an update. Make it clear to them they should do this occasionally, as part of their duty as a covert agent is to know where they stand with their assets.

  • The party may not be aware of everything affecting their Subtlety. Like gauging Subtlety, in some instances, they will have to put time and effort into figuring out what could be affecting their rating. This also allows you to introduce these aspects to your story (especially if the players missed earlier threads or threats against them).

  • Consider introducing narrative elements in the world when their Subtlety Levels change (such as from @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.KbejcPMug5gfoWWz.JournalEntryPage.k3IIBps2ZS9Ap23D#suspicious-(subtlety-7-5)]{Suspicious} to @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.KbejcPMug5gfoWWz.JournalEntryPage.k3IIBps2ZS9Ap23D#overt-(subtlety-4-2)]{Overt}). Do NPCs react to them differently? Do they quickly hear rumours of people searching for them, or perhaps an enemy has detected them and goes deeper into hiding?

pages.name: Signs of Chaos
pages.text:
‘@UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.KN6hJOFxExaZ7fYL#witch-marks-and-other-heresies]{Witch-marks}’ and ‘Marks of Chaos’ are a generic term for things that reveal, or at least hint at, heretical actions on the part of the bearer}. The most obvious are the horrific mutations of Chaos, but there are other types of marks. They may be literal marks, such as tattoos, brands, or similar things inscribed into a heretic’s flesh. Marks of Heresy can also include items worn on the person, such as jewellery or clothing, items of xenos technology, or even implants and augmetics.

Regardless of their nature, to be useful as clues in an investigation or for other game purposes, marks must be distinctive. This does not mean they have to be obvious, of course — a distinctive tattoo could be concealed beneath clothing, or surrounded by other tattoos to obscure it to anyone who does not know to specifically look for it. They do, however, have to be distinct enough to be meaningful to the players once they observe the mark in question.

That distinction may be evident from the game’s lore — for instance, three circles arranged in a triangle is well-known as a Mark of Nurgle. The distinction may also become evident during the course of the game. For example, a brand depicting a hand inscribed in a hexagon may be cryptic at first, but when the players discover this is the mark of the blasphemous cult they are seeking, it will then become distinctive for them.

When you design something intended to be a Mark of Heresy, make sure the players will recognise it or will learn about its significance soon after discovering it. Also, be wary of ‘unintended’ Marks. If you establish that surreptitious cybernetic implants are the Mark of an insidious T’au conspiracy, then be wary of throwing in a ‘casual’ implant. It should either be relevant to the investigation of the conspiracy or deliberately crafted as a red herring. Otherwise, you may send your players on an unintentional diversion from your story.

As always, it is a good idea to establish what constitutes Marks of Heresy in your game when you are crafting them, and plan for their introduction at appropriate points in your story. Identifying a mark requires a Lore (Forbidden Knowledge) Test. But, characters could also use Linguistics (Cypher) or (Forbidden) if the mark in question has language-based affectations, or even Awareness (Sight) if the mark draws in larger aspects, such as hidden within architecture or particular engineering. See @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-journals.JournalEntry.uzQAAUFfkNu8TZOi]{Radical Methods} for further guidance.

Marks of Chaos

Each of the four Chaos Gods is represented by a distinctive mark, a unique glyph whose origins and peculiarities of design are entirely cryptic. A fifth Mark, a glyph representing the undivided ideology of Chaos itself, also exists — the form of an eight-pointed star, thought to represent Chaos’s many paths and possibilities. Given the endlessly jealous acrimony among the Chaos Gods, this Mark is profoundly rare and extremely powerful, as it combines the effects of all four of the other @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-journals.JournalEntry.6hX0E9XlPUoRaDaQ.JournalEntryPage.KN6hJOFxExaZ7fYL#witch-marks-and-other-heresies]{Marks}. You should reserve this particular Mark for extraordinary and particularly powerful villains!

The other form of Chaos ‘Marks’ are the myriad physical, mental, and spiritual mutations inflicted on mortals by its perverse, reality-twisting nature. Since mutations are determined randomly, some will be subtle and easy to conceal, while others will be grossly obvious. This fits with the mercurial nature of Chaos. Tzeentch, for instance, may see fit to bless a heretical adherent with a mutation that will be easy to conceal, allowing them to continue their insidious blasphemy without being detected. However, Tzeentch may likewise twist another heretic into a malformed horror, causing them to be immediately discovered. The schemes of Tzeentch are woven into supremely complex tapestries, however, so it may suit some subtle plot for this particular mortal to be revealed — and probably put immediately to death. The mind and purposes of a Chaos God such as Tzeentch are, after all, unknowable things!

The following sections present some of the more common visual aspects and domains of the Chaos Gods you can use in crafting your adventure’s clues. Pay particular attention to each God’s sacred numbers — the dark gods and their followers often arrange elements of their marks, organisation, and iconography after these numbers, whether consciously or otherwise.

Khorne Clues

Blood for the Blood God, Skulls for the Skull Throne. The Lord of Battles, the Great Butcher. He is the patron of warriors, conflict, hatred, and bloodshed. His influence can be found on battlefields, gladiatorial arenas ,and bloody murder scenes.

  • Khorne’s sacred number is 8

  • Skulls and severed heads, often marked with further sigils

  • Blood sacrifice, bloodletting, blood-painted sigils

  • Depictions or use of bladed weapons, particularly swords and axes

  • Gates as per the teeth of his icon

  • General use of brass or black iron

Nurgle Clues

Grandfather of plagues and pestilence. He is the patron of despair, decay, and disease. His influence can be found festering in the bowels of Humanity, particularly among the sick and ailing. He spreads supernatural maladies, daemonic parasites, and disfiguring mutations.

  • Nurgle’s sacred number is 7

  • His marks can often manifest within the symptoms of disease or illness

  • Tri-lobed designs; particularly bloated spheres arranged in a distorted triangle

  • Insects: mainly flies, worms and grubs

  • Often accompanied by bile, pus, or other sickly fluids.

  • Appears in verdigrised bronze or rusting steel

Slaanesh Clues

Dark Prince of excess and pleasure. He is the patron of desire, obsession, and debasement. His influence can be found among noble courts or wherever inequality presents masters and servants. He spreads greed like a plague, amplifying the desires of the few to subjugate the needs of the many.

  • Slaanesh’s sacred number is 6

  • The symbol often appears directly as so but can manifest in any living material as mutation, such as a pattern of iridescent scales, a knot of pumping veins, or pupils twisted into a new shape

  • Garish colours and contrasting materials, a balance of ostentatiousness and foulness, meant to stand out

  • The brand often represents the Dark Prince’s ownership

  • Often surrounded by excess or acts of vanity

Tzeentch Clues

Changer of Ways and Architect of Fate. He is the patron of sorcery, trickery, and mutation. His influence can be found wherever knowledge gathers or where the longing for change manifests. He operates through esoteric prophecy and the spreading of secrets.

  • Tzeentch’s sacred number is 9

  • Forms of stylised staring eyes, or even methods of surveillance

  • Serpentine Curves, often barbed

  • Many Marks draw on ever-changing aspects: the flow of fire, chemicals, or light

  • Often draws on aspects of cryptonumeracy and numerology

  • Appears in silver or liquid metals

In addition to the @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-tables.RollTable.aHz4wSCM8ogTVOhT]{Mutations} and @UUID[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-core-tables.RollTable.AJC7cYdzY3rIHZWm]{Malignancies} Tables in Imperium Maledictum, you can use the following Marks of Chaos Table to ‘offer’ an even greater array of horrific malformations to your NPCs — and, if they earn them, the players' characters.

@TableHTML[Compendium.navis-apexialis.navis-inquisition-tables.RollTable.2eoGwiPLLyZU1YLe]{Effect}

pages.name: Signs of Xenos
pages.text:
Marks of Heresy reflect the influence of xenos in many diverse ways. They generally reflect the character of the xenos species in question but otherwise represent a collection of physical marks on the body, augments, implants and other biochemical changes, and illicit weapons and other technology. The following Marks do not present an exhaustive list. You can certainly use them in your own games, but you could also use them as inspiration for xenos Marks that better suit your needs.

Aeldari

The Imperium knows very little about the Aeldari other than what the Ordo Xenos has gathered at great expense or through opportune interrogations. From their point of view, the Aeldari remain essentially unknowable aliens, capable of enacting capricious plots and, therefore, not to be trusted. Even their presence in the Macharian Sector is unknown — unlike the more straightforward enemy their Drukhari brethren present, who raid and pirate within Imperial space.

Aeldari trade their goods and services with Humanity only where it benefits them. While they act as invaluable contacts or mercenaries, especially when exploring the unknown parts of the sector, anything traded in their favour is another small foothold against the Imperium. Do not forget that they look down upon Humanity as a lesser species; some foresee an end for Humanity that mirrors the destruction of their own kind, a succumbing to the Ruinous Powers. Some Aeldari fear this, not for the pity of Humanity’s end, but for the resulting galaxy-wide destruction that could swallow up the rest of their kind.

Drukhari

To the twisted, cruel Drukhari, Humans are simply another type of potential captive — or victim. Exploiting the strange netherworld realm known as the Webway, their incursions are usually focused on causing painful bloodshed and taking prisoners to fates that can be literally worse than death. Drukhari collaborators help facilitate these interdimensional raids and cover up their aftermath, paving the way for further raids.

Drukhari collaborators are most likely unwilling in the role, but if the alternative is agonising death or worse, then the heresy of collaboration may seem the lesser of evils. If the Drukhari choose to mark their reluctant confederates, it will invariably be in a painful way — brands and amputations are common. Likewise, Drukhari may provide potent drugs to their ‘allies’, granting them temporary, superhuman abilities. But the cost is predictably terrible, as these drugs are designed for Drukhari physiology and are likely to inflict crippling addiction and other side effects on Humans.

The Leagues of Votann

The Kin of the Leagues of Votann are often known to the Imperium by the somewhat pejorative term ‘Squats’, and many believe their classification varies between abhuman and true xenos. As such, they are often mistaken for harmless citizens of the Imperium, but acolytes of the Inquisition should always err on the side of classifying the kin as outright xenos. Their culture represents as much of an existential threat to the Imperium as any other xenos culture — their supposedly superior technology is clearly outside the God-Emperor’s and Omnissiah’s sanction, especially the rumoured living machines that co-exist with them.

To the Inquisition, the exact scale of empire the Leagues of Votann represent is yet to be fully understood. They have only recorded encounters with minor scouting and prospecting fleets at the edges of the Imperium. However, some League representatives are smart enough to avoid Inquisition detection. Some are eager to accept mercenary and simple trade contracts with representatives of the Imperium as a practical means to garner wealth and, more insidiously, intelligence on Imperial assets.

Necrons

A soulless machine species that despises all living things, the Necrons are unlikely to willingly deal with Human collaborators. To the extent that they will do anything but attempt to destroy life that gets in their way, they may at least initially attempt some infiltration. Awakening a tomb world and preparing it for battle takes time, and any information gained in the meantime could be useful to ensure victory.

When Necrons seek to control an enemy species, they use strange implants or devices known as ‘mindshackle scarabs’ to override and influence people’s behaviours. Their stiff, stilted manner might trigger an acolyte’s suspicion, with the revelation of implanted tech confirming their altered nature. Perhaps more dangerous is the very allure of their mysterious technology, drawing the attention of hereteks and those susceptible to techheresy. These heretics toy with powers beyond their comprehension, unaware or ignorant of the collateral damage their experiments are sure to produce.

T'au Empire

T’au infiltration into the Imperium is not uncommon. Dedicated to pursuing their foul ‘greater good’, T’au leaders often try to recruit spies and other agents among the native population of a planet or system they seek to add to their Empire. Swayed by gifts of advanced technology and possibly promised great power under a new T’au regime, such confederates may provide their T’au handlers with information, or even engage in acts of sabotage. The point, of course, is to pave the way for a subsequent T’au incursion, or even an outright invasion of Humanity’s space.

The most likely Marks indicative of a T’au intrusion into the Imperium is suspiciously advanced tech in the hands of Imperial citizens. Sophisticated scanners and recording devices used for spying, clandestine communications gear, and characteristic T’au pulse weapons are all possible things to implicate someone in collaboration with the T’au. Regarding behaviour, watch for talk about their ‘greater good’ or any vast open-mindedness on display. Inquisition reports suggest that the T’au Ethereal caste has been experimenting with broadening pheromone-based control to afflict other species, including Humans.

Orks

Orks are rarely interested in other species’ cultures, generally preferring a good punch-up over subtle or insidious infiltration that other species may attempt. However, some Warbosses enjoy scheming, so they may infiltrate Human settlements to seek targets and resources. They are scavengers — signs of their presence often result in effigies made of scrap, various gubbins welded or bolted on, miscellaneous glyphs, and brutish sigils otherwise painted or scratched into the original item.

Tyranids

Tyranids are ravening, existential horrors that exist solely to consume. Within the Imperium, a subset of heretics worships these monsters, working within targeted worlds to pave the way for a subsequent invasion by a Tyranid Hive Fleet. These so-called Genestealer Cults insert themselves into the doomed society, sowing chaos and spreading the gospels of false xenos gods. If they successfully establish a firm foothold, then their psychic emanations aim to draw the nearest hive fleet to consume the world, cultists and all.

Genestealer Cults are profoundly secret societies. Their highest ranking members are often vile hybrids of Human and xenos genetics. They seek to exploit Human fears, desires, and other weaknesses to draw adherents to their ranks. Hybrid cultists are generally obvious, so tend to remain out of sight, but later generations may appear Human enough to remain undetected by the naked eye.

Genestealer Cult Symbology

Like Chaos cults, Genestealer Cults work with an established pattern in their symbology and cyphers.   • Most cults have their own variant of the coiling, insecto-serpentine glyph known as the wyrm-form.

  • This wyrm-form can be expressed in hidden tattoos or graffiti to mark territories or send warnings to other cultists.

  • Talismanic variants of the wyrm-form icon can appear in modified weaponry, even in functional aspects, the curve sharpened into a blade.

  • As cults rise in an area, they will brazenly deface Imperial iconography with their own. This can be a sign that their uprising is soon to begin.
